item.title: Knicks make final roster decision on James Wiseman, Bruce Brown
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: The New York Knicks made their final roster move of the preseason on Saturday, waiving veteran guard Bruce Brown as they finalized their group for the 2026-27 season.Obviously, the decision clears the way for former No. 2 overall pick James Wiseman to remain on the regular-season roster before the campaign gets going on Tuesday.Wiseman averaged 8.0 points and 4.3 rebounds across four preseason appearances after joining New York on an Exhibit 9 training camp deal. The Knicks are now expected to convert that agreement into a league-minimum contract.New York needed additional frontcourt depth after Mitchell Robinson left in free agency for the Boston Celtics and Ariel Hukporti departed to join the Philadelphia 76ers. The Knicks added Andre Drummond as their primary backup center behind Karl-Anthony Towns, and Wiseman is now positioned to provide another option as the third-string center.Wiseman, however, has played only five NBA games over the past two seasons with Indiana. His last extended run came with Detroit in 2023-24, when he averaged 7.1 points and 5.3 rebounds across 63 appearances.It’s fair to say the former Golden State Warriors lottery pick did enough during preseason to secure a spot as New York’s reserve center depth and convince Mike Brown he deserved the final roster spot.Brown, meanwhile, will become a free agent after spending last season with the Denver Nuggets, where he appeared in all 82 games and averaged 7.9 points, 3.9 rebounds and 2.1 assists… only to fail to get a guaranteed deal this summer.Good luck, Bruce, and welcome to New York (now for good), James!

item.title: 'Getting back to this point has been a journey of its own' - Fem van Empel one spot off podium at Berencross on return to racing
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Fifty weeks ago Fem van Empel last pinned on a race number. The three-time cyclo-cross World Champion then walked away from racing for an extended break. On Saturday, she returned to action at the C2 Berencross in Meulebeke with a fresh setup for cyclo-cross, Specialized TMRW, and a fresh reboot to her burgeoning career. "It’s been nearly a year since my last race, and getting back to this point has been a journey of its own. Taking a step back wasn't easy, but I am incredibly proud of the choices I’ve made. Looking forward to racing again! Let's have some fun. See you tomorrow," she posted to Instagram.And the young Dutch rider jumped into the mud and the fray again, working her way around the West Flanders course in Meulebeke for fourth place.In late October last year, the 23-year-old Dutch rider celebrated her 50th career victory in cyclo-cross, winning in the mud at Exact Cross Heerderstrand. A week later she stopped racing during Koppenbergcross and then took time off "for my mental health and well-being", leading to a permanent separation from her Visma-Lease a Bike team.The three-time cyclo-cross World Champion, a free agent to start 2026, confirmed a contract with FDJ United-Suez in September as her "new adventure", the French Women's WorldTour squad registering a new cyclo-cross team for the 2026-2027 season, Specialized TMRW."I took the time to recover. And I have been happier than ever since. I have traveled a lot. In doing so, I got to know myself in a different way. I wouldn't have missed this for the world," she said prior to Beremcross to , the Flemish-speaking broadcaster, which was reported by ."I had lost the joy of cycling. I was no longer able to pursue top-level sport in the way I would like." Marie Schreiber rode away from the field and continued her streak of podiums in early-season C2 cyclo-cross races with a third victory in four starts. Behind the Luxembourg rider, a wave of Dutch riders filled the next eight spots, Anik van Alpen (777TV CX) in second and Lucinda Brand (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) in third, with Van Empel sprinting ahead of Ceylin Del Carmen Alvarado (Fenix-Premier Tech)."The number of times I have been on a cyclo-cross bike this year can be counted on the fingers of one hand. It takes a bit of getting used to starting here again. It won't all look as stylish as it should today. But I am taking the time to work on that as well," she said.Van Empel was the first of the four riders to debut with Specialized TMRW this season, other teammates Anja Grossmann, Amandine Muller and Célia Gery yet to start their cyclo-cross seasons. Last year Gery earned the women's U23 bronze medal at Cyclo-cross World Championships in Hulst, while Muller was fifth, both racing for France.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 2026 Yankees Team LVP: Ryan McMahon
item.author: Peter Brody
item.content:encoded: In truth, the decision for the Least Valuable Player of the 2026 Yankees only ever boiled down to two players. The two standout candidates for this ignominious award were Ryan McMahon and Trent Grisham, and for very similar reasons. In addition to their black hole bats polluting the lineup, there was apprehension from the start that they could ever provide the amount of value commensurate with the amount of money they were earning. The pair combined to cost the Yankees a hair over $38 million in 2026 — 11.3-percent of their estimated $335.8 million luxury tax payroll — and yet combined to produce just 1.2 fWAR, or a measly 2.8-percent of the team’s 43.1 overall fWAR. McMahon narrowly edges Grisham for the distinction for the 20-point gap in their wRC+ (78 vs. 98) and regression in the one area where he was supposed to excel: defense.When it became apparent that a key cog of Operation Run It Back concerned persisting with McMahon as the team’s starting third baseman, the mental gymnastics required to rationalize this decision began tying fans’ minds in knots. “If the Yankees can find a way to help his bat take advantage of the Yankee Stadium short porch and bring it closer to league average production, this along with his reliably stellar defense at the hot corner creates a player with plenty of value to the 2026 team,” was a common refrain. The problem with this wishful thinking became immediately obvious when you realize that McMahon has never posted a league average or better season at the plate by wRC+ despite playing the first eight-and-a-half seasons of his career at Coors field, rendering the belief that you could suddenly transform a 31-year-old hitter into something he had never been a folly. McMahon’s season began worse than even the most pessimistic fan could have predicted with just a 51 wRC+ and 33-percent strikeout rate through the end of April. The walk rate that had provided a nominal floor of offensive value was drying up and he was bleeding bat speed, leading to a tweak in the width of his batting stance that provided a modest improvement but still nothing close to the 91 wRC+ hitter he had been over the previous five seasons. McMahon missed 38 games after dealing with a late-June throat infection and a mid-August Grade 2 thumb sprain, but by that point was already ceding reps at third to a pair of ostensibly worse defenders in José Caballero and Amed Rosario. The Gold Glove caliber defense which convinced the Yankees to acquire him from the Rockies at the 2025 trade deadline had deserted him. It got to the point where the Yankees were giving practice reps to Anthony Volpe at the hot corner — a position he had never played in his professional career — in the days leading up to the playoffs. It culminated in a play which really summarized his season in a nutshell, McMahon booting a routine grounder from Yandy Díaz, the first batter the Rays sent to the plate in Game 2 of the ALDS. That error started an avalanche of defensive miscues that ended with four errors in an ugly 5-2 loss. For a player brought in for his defense, it begged the question “what do you even do here?” McMahon rode the bench in Game 3 as the Yankees got swept, bringing an end to possibly the worst season of his big league career when combining all the factors. He finished with a putrid .213/.279/.357 triple slash line, with 11 home runs, 41 RBIs, a 78 wRC+, and 0.5 fWAR in 360 plate appearances across 124 games. His .279 OBP and 78 wRC+ placed him among the 20 worst hitters in MLB with at least 350 PAs in 2026. His 11 home runs, 78 wRC+, 7.8-percent walk rate, zero Statcast Outs Above Average, and 0.5 fWAR were all the lowest marks of his career since the COVID-shortened season of 2020 and easily the worst marks of any season in which he played at least 100 games. He also cannot be separated from the broader context of the team. His presence on the roster emboldened the Yankees to re-up with Rosario over the winter to reprise his platoon partner role. That turned into an unmitigated disaster, Rosario immediately forgetting how to hit against lefties — the one thing he was supposed to be good at — while producing an almost impossibly bad -7 OAA in just 394 innings, his seven errors at third coming in moments that contributed to costing the Yankees a shot at the division. The most disheartening aspect of the whole charade is that everybody could see it coming. It is therefore not so much an indictment on McMahon — a known quantity who happened to regress in the one area where he still provided some value — as it is on the Yankees front office for allowing third base to remain a perennial black hole. In the words of our fearless leader Andrew Mearns, it all started with “the original sin of giving DJ LeMahieu six years to save on taxable AAV.” Since signing LeMahieu to that second contract prior to the start of the 2021 season, eleven players have taken at least 100 plate appearances while manning third base for the Yankees. Below is a breakdown of the amount of guaranteed money paid out to each of those players and the offensive production and value they provided:It total, the Yankees have paid out $222.5 million to players who have soaked up the majority of playing time at the hot corner. The 89 wRC+ those players have returned ranks 21st in baseball while the 11.5 fWAR is only a touch better in 19th place. Plenty of teams have committed nine-figure sums to the position during that span — Manny Machado, Rafael Devers, Nolan Arenado, Anthony Rendon, Carlos Correa, Austin Riley, Alex Bregman, José Ramírez, Matt Chapman, and Kevin McGonigle have all signed deals in excess of $150 million — but outside of Rendon and Correa no team gets a consistently worse return on the amount of money they invest in third base than the Yankees. McMahon is just the latest figurehead of this maddening trend. The Yankees owe him $16 million in 2027. After a disastrous 2026 campaign, the question for McMahon is not whether he can fulfill that outlay with value on the field. It’s whether the Yankees will follow a similar path as they did with LeMahieu in 2025, Aaron Hicks in 2023, and Jacoby Ellsbury in 2019 and cut bait this offseason, eating the dead money for the privilege of not having to subject fans to his poor play.

item.title: Big Sugar Gravel: Kongstad and Hobbs Claim the Final Gravel Crowns of the Year
item.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
item.content:encoded: Keegan Swenson and Sofia Gomez Villafañe took the overall Life Time Grand Prix series wins.

item.title: Life Time Grand Prix: Stella Hobbs uses long-range solo attack to win elite women's Big Sugar Gravel
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Stella Hobbs (MAAP-ENVE) soloed to victory in the elite women's gravel race at Big Sugar Classic in Bentonville, Arkansas on Saturday. From a four-rider chase group, Sofia Gomez Villafañe (Specialized Off-road) won the sprint for second and Hayley Preen (ChemChamp Honeycomb) secured third. Karolina Migoń (PAS Racing) jumped early to the front before the final left-hand bend that led to the uphill straightaway, and she finished fifth, passed at the end by Kylee Hanel (Cervelo-Maxxis).The race was the sixth and final event in the Life Time Grand Prix. Overall leader Villafañe took a 12-point lead into the race and added to that margin to win her fourth series title in five years. Preen secured her second place overall with her third-place finish, while Hobbs moved up to 12th overall. Last year in the storm-shortened Arkansas event, Hobbs finished third. The year before on the traditional 100-plus mile route, she finished seventh. A podium spot was a target to make a big move from 12th in the series into the top 10, where the season-ending prize purse of $350,000 would be shared among women and men. "I have often said here I would just really like to see the front of the race finish. I've always wanted that, and that can be a really good motivator," Hobbs told organisers at the finish."When I broke away over the top of the 'power line' climb, I thought, maybe. And then I quickly backed myself down from that. Then we have those two paved climbs into the finish, and I did not believe that I would get over the top of both of those without getting caught, until I was through [the climbs and final corners], and then I finally believed I could win it."This is my favourite race on the calendar. I would say the first half I wasn't so sure if it would be my favourite race of the day. We just had such a big group, and I kind of lost track of myself and didn't really know what I should be doing or where I should be. But by the second half, I remembered how much I love it here."Villafañe said the race was made in the second half, where climbing was more substantial at a 24% gradient along a rough road after the final checkpoint and riders had to overcome tired legs. "You start to have a lot of climbs, and you had Paige [Onweller] really looking to animate the race, and Karo [Migoń] was animating, and so was I. The group just slowly started to whittle down, whittle down, and really going into the second feed zone, Stella was really, really pushing the pace, and I was like, I think this girl has winning legs today. But I didn't want to quite tell her that."I was hoping to make it up the power line climb with her, and then be able to go. We tried really hard to bring Stella back and we couldn't."Super hard day. It was actually very, very tactical. I am super happy to have a good ride," Villafañe told Life Time broadcast at the finish. One of the surprising moves of the day came from Hanel, the U23 leader in the Life Time Grand Prix who stayed with the elites to the end. The result should give her the women's U23 title. A total of 18 of the top 20 riders in Big Sugar were part of the Life Time Grand Prix.A total of 53 women took the early-morning start in Bentonville 10 minutes after the elite men. The front group held together across the early 30 miles of mixed terrain in northwest Arkansas, crossing into Missouri, with Morgan Aguirre (PAS Racing), Hannah Otto (Scott Sports USA) and the stars-and-stripes of US gravel national champion Paige Onweller (Trek Driftless) at the front. The climbing picked up beyond the first aid station in Pineville, and New Zealander Charlotte Clarke took a flyer after two hours of racing.With under 55 miles to go, Clarke's escapade was over and she found herself in a chasing group behind a new lead pack, Villafañe with Onweller, Migoń, Cecile Lejeune (Trek Driftless), Hobbs, Preen, and Sarah Lange, as well as women's U23 rivals Samanth Johnson (Lunchbox Racing) and Hanel. Heading to the final checkpoint near Washburn, Missouri at Rockford Grange, the lead group hit out on one of the rougher roads with a two-minute margin on solo attacker Lauren De Crescenzo. There was a 1:20 gap to the next group of chasers, which included Johnson, Agurirre, Alexis Skarda, Danni Shrosbree, Haley Smith, Ruby Ryan, Samara Sheppard, Emma Langley and Decker. Otto had fallen off the pace, riding in 19th position.Six riders - Villafane, Hobbs, Onweller, Preen, Migon and Lejeune rolled through Rockford Grange in a long line as they took final hydration, none stopping for technical assistance. Lange dangled about 10 seconds back with Hanel close by. They were all together once on a short paved section.Back on gravel, on a steep climb with loose dirt and rocks, Hobbs punched hard and gained a little gap, as a few riders swerved and tried to stay upright behind, now in chase mode. She gained 25 seconds at the top of the climb, and another 33 seconds across the next 10 miles, leaving 15 miles to go.Hobbs continued to build her lead and never saw the chasers in her rear view, gliding across the pavement at the finish line with her first Life Time event victory.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Penalty sets up epic Verstappen charge in his GT return
item.author: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen's return to GT racing in the pause between Formula 1 grands prix featured plenty of drama, an eventual top-10 finish, and brought a huge audience (both online and at the track) to the Portimao GT World Challenge event.A set-up miscue had left the Verstappen team's 2 Seas Motorsport-run Mercedes scraping its way to just 15th on the grid in a shower of sparks during Friday evening's qualifying session.Verstappen's team-mates Ben Barnicoat and Chris Lulham made rapid progress forward as they took the first two stints, with Barnicoat soon into the top 10 and Lulham charging towards the top five when he took the wheel.But Lulham then incurred a drivethrough penalty for assisting Luca Stolz's Mercedes into a spin as he tried to take fifth on a restart lap following a safety car.Lulham took that penalty just before handing over to Verstappen, who therefore took over down in 24th place with just 45 minutes of after-dark racing to go.Another long safety car cost Verstappen some racing laps to make up ground but did at least close the pack up.There were 23 minutes left at the restart, with Verstappen 19th by then. He produced a spectacular charge forward that included a particularly entertaining battle with Charles Leclerc's brother Arthur in an AF Corse Ferrari, and managed to at least salvage a top-10 finish in ninth.That was enough to prompt a massive grin from Verstappen as he got back to the pits, and a huge cheer from the crowd in the main grandstand.The GetSpeed Mercedes of Ralf Aron, Fabian Schiller and Maxi Gotz took victory.

item.title: Did the Yankees not have a plan against Drew Rasmussen?
item.author: Kento Mizuno
item.content:encoded: If you’re choosing not to watch the rest of the MLB postseason, I don’t blame you at all. However, something interesting happened in Game 2 of the NLCS, something that prompted me to reflect on the Yankees’ performance (or lack of) against the Rays.Down 1-0 against the Brewers, the Dodgers started Yoshinobu Yamamoto to try and even up the series. Yamamoto, if you recall, pitched a complete game against those same Brewers in Game 2 of last year’s NLCS, a first-pitch Jackson Chourio homer the sole blemish on his ledger. This year, however, the Brewers were ready. Taking full advantage of a slightly off Yamamoto, they worked counts and grinded at-bats, chasing him after 2.2 innings, 75 pitches, and 3 runs allowed. Milwaukee went on to win 7-4, completing their revenge.Here was an example of a smart team beating an excellent pitcher who had confounded them in the past. Contrast this with how the Yankees utterly folded against Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 of the ALDS. Why couldn’t the Yankees do as the Brewers did?Now, I realize that overcoming elite pitching is a tall ask. It’s possible that not even the Brewers could have solved Rasmussen based on how good he looked that night. However, what irks me isn’t the end result, but the process. The Yankees had seen Rasmussen quite recently; he’d beaten the Bombers to clinch the division for the Rays on September 22. The Tampa Bay ace used the same gameplan for ALDS Game 1. However, the Yankees appeared to have done no homework, looking completely unprepared to counter his approach. Rasmussen’s style of pitching can be summed up as: throw strikes that are hard to punish. The first part is easy to quantify. This year, 49.7% of his pitches landed in the strike zone, while the league average was 41.5%. He likes to attack batters early, as he ran a 67.1% first-strike rate (league average was 61.4%). Consequently, Rasmussen is extremely stingy about issuing free passes: his 4.8% walk rate placed him in the 97th percentile among all pitchers this season. This is a guy that is comfortable challenging hitters in the zone.It’s the second part that sets Rasmussen apart from mere strike-throwers. The Rays ace has both the stuff (110 Stuff+) and command (106 Location+) to avoid damage while challenging hitters. While he is generally average at getting whiffs and avoiding contact, he limits barrels and hard contact extremely well (79th and 83rd percentile, respectively), and generates grounders at a comfortably above average clip (65th percentile). This is not someone you go hacking against. Rasmussen’s strengths were on full display in that September 22 start. Rasmussen pitched 6.2 innings of 1-run ball, striking out 11 in the process. Of the 114 pitches he threw that day, 45.6% were in the strike zone, down from his season average but still above league average. However, the Yankees flailed helplessly against his stuff, making contact only 35 times out of 53 swings for an abysmal 66% contact rate. Even when they did make contact, it was mostly harmless. The Yankees managed just two hard-hit balls in fair territory against Rasmussen, both by Heliot Ramos of all people: a 107.3 mph lineout in the fourth, and a 110.5 mph double in the seventh. I count only two positives from that outing for the Yankees: they managed to make Rasmussen throw 114 pitches, and they coaxed three walks out of him. Other than that, they got schooled.Now, I’m not going to sit here and tell you that the Yankees just needed to do X, Y, and Z to solve Rasmussen. There are no obvious answers to counter a guy this good. But at the same time, business as usual doesn’t cut it, either. If you’re trying to win against elite pitching in October, you need a team-wide, concerted approach. For what it’s worth, if I was calling the shots, I would have instructed the Yankees to be extremely passive. I would have implored them to run deep counts, wait for mistakes, and to avoid expanding the zone at all costs. Groundbreaking, I know. But at least this puts pressure on Rasmussen to consistently execute, and while he’s a great pitcher, he’s not a robot. This strategy is also rooted in an honest appraisal of the Yankees’ strengths and weaknesses at the plate: they sucked at making contact (75.1% contact rate, 27th in MLB), but they were above average at avoiding chase (31.9 O-Swing%, 9th best). And if nothing else, this would have likely meant a higher pitch count for Rasmussen. Yes, he throws strikes, but more than half of his pitches still land outside the strike zone. Laying off those even once per at-bat would have resulted in a markedly higher pitch total for Rasmussen, forcing the Rays to go to their bullpen earlier.However, the Yankees did none of that in Game 1 of the ALDS. Instead, they went up hacking. Their overall swing rate was 50.4%, up from their season average of 46.3%. They kept chasing pitches out of the strike zone; their O-Swing% for the night was 36.5%, much higher than their seasonal mark. They made contact on those pitches just 39.1% of the time, with their overall contact rate dipping to a truly pitiful 60.3%. All this chase and whiff prevented the Yankees from being able to run deep counts; of the 25 plate appearances against Rasmussen that night, 10 ended in three pitches or fewer. And that’s how they let Rasmussen dominate them for 8 innings and 101 pitches. Again, I’m not saying that the Yankees would have easily solved Rasmussen if only they had been a bit more patient. They ran up his pitch count to 114 on September 22, and he still ended up limiting them to one run. What irritates me is the perceived lack of strategy. Surely, they had to have known about Rasmussen’s strengths. They should have known their own strengths and weaknesses as a team. Why, then, was their plan to just swing away?I don’t have any insight on the inner workings of the Yankees’ organization. Maybe they were planning on being more patient against Rasmussen, but the plan was just executed poorly. Or maybe their increased aggressiveness was a conscious strategy based on internal data I don’t have access to. But watching Game 1, I couldn’t shake the feeling that the Yankees’ batters were just going up there with no real plan other than “try to hit ball”. It makes you wonder how the Yankees approached advance scouting and preparation for that all-important game – or whether they did so at all.

item.title: Life Time Grand Prix: Tobias Kongstad surges from nine-rider sprint to win elite men's gravel race at Big Sugar Classic
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Tobias Mørch Kongstad (PAS Racing) led out a nine-rider sprint and won the Life Time 2026 Big Sugar Classic gravel race on Saturday in Bentonville, Arkansas. The third-placed finisher at this year's Unbound Gravel 200 was part of an early breakaway and then chased back to the lead pack to take the win in 4:36:03. He finished ahead of a pair of Life Time Grand Prix contenders, Mārtiņš Blūms (Velo Express) taking second and Cole Paton (Giant-RCC) in third. Cole Davis (SpeedStudio-Basso), like Kongstad not looking for Grand Prix points, was one second back in fourth. The next four spots were filled by Grand Prix contenders, Matt Wilson (Scott Sports USA) going fifth, Drew Dillman sixth, Brendan Johnston (Giant) seventh and Andreas Seewald (Singer KTM Racing) eighth. Gliding across the line at the back of the bunch in ninth was former collegiate racer Henry Nelson (Lunchbox Racing).The race was the sixth and final event in the Life Time Grand Prix. Overall leader Keegan Swenson (Specialized Off-road) had an early mechanical that hindered his catch of front groups and he finished 3:41 off the pace, 24th overall. His 13th place finish in the Grand Prix provided enough of a margin for him to take back the overall title, just one point ahead of Johnston."I just tried my best in the sprint, and sometimes your best is enough. And yeah, it was good," Kongstad told organisers at the finish, not thinking about the series at all.He escaped early and led much of the first half of the 101.4-mile race with Hayden Christian (Trek Driftless-MAAP), as the two lost a third partner, John Borstelmann (Ventum), to a mechanical. "I'm just lucky that my competitors still allow me to go into breakaway. I got caught at the bottom of a super steep climb out there, and that was not the best. But I tried to manage my effort before I got caught, so I was not fully cooked."So from there on, I think I played a technical game, saying to guys, "Hey guys, I've been in breakaway all day. I cannot pull'. Luckily, I convinced them. Sometimes you just need to play your cards right."Blūms admitted he went off course early in the race and rode with Simon Pellaud (Cervelo-Assos-Maxxis) to get back to a big group. He was the top finisher in the Grand Prix at the race."I was with Pellaud way back behind the big bunch because he got a flat. I took the wrong turn. I had to turn back, and we didn't see the front group, so I had no clue what's happening in the front at all. We catched the front just before the first aid station. So we burned matches quite a lot to get there," he told Life Time livestream cameras."I was just trying to recover. I was struggling a lot at some point, but yeah, somehow I got in the rhythm. I tried to attack a couple times before the finish, and there were still some guys interested to chase me down. "I just tried to stay more in the front because we were quite a big bunch there. At the finish last corners, I was still in the front there, so I just went on a couple of wheels and made my way through the bunch to second."The first shakeout of the day came from Brendan Johnston (Giant) and Matthew Wilson (Scott Sports USA), who moved away from the peloton in the first dozen miles but it was all back together with 80 miles to go as the first moderate climb led riders across the Arkansas state line into Missouri.With 62 miles to go, a group of three riders had driven away and carved out a one minute gap - Kongstad, Borstelmann and Christian. Pellaud was back in the pack of chasers, having had to deal with a mechanical in the first 30km. He rode with Cole Paton, Bradyn Lange, Brendan Johnston, Matt Wilson, Alexey Vermeulen, Andreas Seewald and Cobe Freeburn, among the favourites.Borstelmann then had a mechanical and had to stop on the side of the road, leaving Christian and Kongstad to set the pace. The duo held a 1:13 lead passing the checkpoint with under 50 miles to go. Chasing were 39 riders in a large pack, led by Cameron Jones (Scott Sports USA-RCC), last year's Grand Prix overall winner who was looking to get back into the top 10 at this final race. Meanwhile, current overall Grand Prix leader Swenson was in 46th position, three-and-a-half minutes back, having suffered a mechanical early on and stopping for a wheel swap in an aid station.The most northern part of the course completed, the two leaders carried only 40 seconds as they moved southward toward the second and final checkpoint near Washburn, Missouri at Rockford Grange, riding one of the rougher roads on the route.Kongstad's lead was precarious, as with less than 27 miles to go Christian joined forces with seven others and began to close down the gap. Swenson was 2:40 back, making up some time.One of the steepest climbs of the day, with 24% gradients, followed with 23 miles to go across the top and soon Kongstad was no longer alone. He drove on with 20 miles to go in a group with a pack that included Christian along with Seewald, Drew Dillman, Blums, Daxton Mock and Pellaud. Behind the new configuration of leaders by 50 seconds loomed Johnston with Cole Davis, Ryker Brand, Henry Nelson, Nathan Spratt and Wilson. More favourites were just another 20 back of that group, including Paton, Freeburn, and Jones.Now back in Arkansas on some fast descents, six riders remained together at the front - Dillman, Blums, Mock, Seewald, Kongstad and Pellaud. Six others trailed by 32 seconds, kicking up the dusty doubletrack with 15 miles to go, and across the next few miles the two groups merged.With 8 miles to go, Nelson gave it a go with a solo attack, now mixing with the 50-mile rider traffic. He carried his momentum onto the pavement and uphill section back to downtown Bentonville, the chasers not panicked as the former University of Arkansas rider was not in the Grand Prix. With 2 miles to go and going past the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art entrance, Nelson looked back and could sense the big favourites getting close. In the final mile he relented and was part of the final drag race, won by Kongstad.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Yankees Arizona Fall League Week 2 Recap
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: We’re two weeks down in the annual pilgrimage to the desert, and it’s been an up-and-down experience for the Yankees’ contingent and the rest of the Salt River Rafters. A very strong opening week shifted to a more challenging second week, one that saw several prospects struggle. As a reminder, if you want a quick rundown on who’s in the desert this month, check here.October 9 (Rafters 13, Desert Dogs 9): Salt River started a rough week with a high-scoring win over Glendale, one where they led 7-1 after two innings. Only one Yankee got into a game, as Core Jackson walked thrice, hit a 100 mph single, and stole a base. He hasn’t had a great time in the desert through two weeks, but he’s shown flashes.October 10 (Rafters 2, Scorpions 10): The pitching didn’t have a good week across the Salt River roster, but the main difference on Saturday was the lack of offense. It wasn’t really the fault of any Yankee, as Kyle West was the only one to play, and he walked in all three at-bats. The issues we saw with the pitching, though, involved Antonio Gomez. He started the sixth with a strikeout, but would allow three hits and two walks before being pulled with two outs. In the end, all five runners he allowed would score. Mack Estrada got the last three outs of the blowout loss in a solid outing.October 13 (Rafters 6, Desert Dogs 5): The Rafters were off on Sunday and saw their game rained out on Monday, an extreme rarity out in Arizona. When they returned on Tuesday, three Yankees got into the game. Dax Kilby made his first appearance of the week, but went 0-for-4, albeit with a pair of stolen bases. Jackson went 1-for-4 with a couple of hard-hit balls, a walk, and two stolen bases. Chris Veach made his first appearance of the series, allowing one run in two innings.October 14 (Rafters 3, Solar Sox 7): On Wednesday, the Rafters put themselves in an early four-run hole and never bounced back. Kilby went 0-for-3 with a walk on a quiet night, albeit with a 108.7 mph groundout. West went 0-for-3 with an RBI and a walk, while Anthony Mena made his lone appearance of the week with a choppy 1.2 innings.October 15 (Rafters 9, Solar Sox 14): It was a light-night barnburner on Thursday night, as the Rafters led 9-8 in the ninth before a game-tying two-out infield single against Gomez tied the game. A five spot in the 10th after a small army of walks doomed them. Jackson went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts, a stolen base, and a run scored. West entered as a late defensive replacement and hit a 103 mph groundout in the ninth. Estrada got two of the three batters he faced out, and while Gomez allowed two hits and had a blown save, he struck out a batter in a “scoreless” inning. He also tried out a new curveball.October 16 (Rafters 0, Javelinas 10): What a crummy way to end the week. You can’t completely blame the Yankees for this one, though. Kilby went 2-for-4 with a 105 mph double, Jackson went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts, and West went 0-for-3 with a strikeout. On the pitching side, we saw JT Etheridge strike out six in an up-and-down 3.1-inning start, while Veach struck out the side in order in the seventh.7-24, HR, 6 RBI, 4 2B, 2 BB, 3 K, 2 SB 3-22, 2B, 5 BB, 9 K, 6 SB 5-23, 5 RBI, 4 BB, 6 K, SB6 IP, 5 H, 3 R (2 ER), 3 BB, 9 K3.1 IP, 2 H, 1 R, 3 BB, 2 K6 IP, 3 H, 3 R, 4 BB, 8 K 5 IP, 6 H, 3 R (2 ER), 2 BB, 6 K 2.2 IP, 5 H, 5 R, 3 BB, 3 K

item.title: Thoughts on the ABS challenge system
item.author: Dani Mohr
item.content:encoded: The Automated Ball Strike (ABS) Challenge System was newly implemented in the majors this season and changed the game for the better. José Caballero made MLB history on Opening Night, tapping his helmet after a questionable strike call to trigger the very first ABS challenge during the Yankees’ season opener against the Giants. Although the challenge was unsuccessful—as was a bit of a trend with Caballero in particular—the ball landed in the top right corner of the zone to uphold the call, it catalyzed a pivotal improvement to the game for the better. Cementing the historic moment in baseball history, Caballero’s helmet is set to be displayed at the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown.Tested for much of the decade at various levels of the minor leagues, the system tracks the specific location of each pitch, relative to the batter’s zone, which is calibrated to his height and measured to the fraction of an inch. Not meant to replace human umpires entirely, it’s meant to primarily correct human error in obvious misses. However, in cases where the call is challenged and upheld, it puts teams in difficult situations as they lose a challenge opportunity for the remainder of the game.The Yankees consistently used their allotted two challenges per game to their advantage and ended the regular season with a 54.7-percent total success rate, with Austin Wells proving to be especially adept at it behind the plate. Experimenting with the system early in the season, the Yankees were more aggressive with challenges and quickly accumulated a high success rate, overturning 10 of 11 calls in their first four games of the season. They were more successful on pitcher/catcher challenges, and Wells finished the regular season with the fourth-highest win percentage from the field.The days of adhering to calls from pitcher-friendly and hitter-friendly umpires, and even from some with personal animosities, will soon be behind us as we expect more modifications to the system. The Pinstripe Alley community shared their thoughts on the topic, and it appears that the majority have more positive feedback on the challenge system and engaged in discussions on how it can improve going forward. Some envision the league allowing three challenges per game, giving teams more opportunities to overturn questionable calls, and others support having at least one challenge available per inning. It will be very interesting to see the evolution of this challenge system within the majors, and it’s already made a lasting impact on the league.

item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Red Rolfe
item.author: Nick Power
item.content:encoded: “They talk about all the other fellas on that team, but I notice the man who hurts us when it counts is that third baseman. There is a real ballplayer.”The Athletics entered the 1930s as the class of the American League, winning their second straight World Series title in ‘30 and taking the pennant again in ‘31. But the decade would belong to another team, one that rebuild itself after the departure of the game’s brightest star. Led by Lou Gehrig and Bill Dickey and, later, Joe DiMaggio and Joe Gordon, with Red Ruffing and Lefty Gomez in the rotation, that incarnation of the Bronx Bombers won four straight championships to close out the decade. But, when asked to identify the most dangerous player on the club, legendary A’s manager and owner Connie Mack named none of those Hall of Famers. Instead, it was the team’s cerebral, ultra-consistent third baseman who Mack feared most. October 17, 1908 (Penacook, NH) July 8, 1969 (Gilford, NH)1931, 1934-42Growing up in New Hampshire, Red Rolfe quickly distinguished himself in both academics and athletics. He earned acceptance to Dartmouth, where he performed well enough to draw the attention of several big-league teams. Mack offered the youngster a tryout, but he ended up signing with the Yankees, who pitched him on the potential to play alongside Gehrig and Babe Ruth.Rolfe would get his chance before long, appearing in a single game as a defensive replacement a few months after his signing in 1931. He’d spend the next two years with the Double-A Newark Bears, consistently hitting for average while continuing to hone his defensive skills on the left side of the infield. He wouldn’t return to the Show until ‘34, when he broke camp with the Yankees. Rolfe’s first year in pinstripes was a mixed bag, as he dealt with maladies and a position switch from shortstop to third due to a lack of arm strength. Still, he immediately impressed some of his more seasoned teammates. “I never saw a kid with so much spirit and desire to learn as Rolfe has shown me,” said Gehrig. “When you start to discuss things, this Rolfe sticks his ear right into your tonsils. He wants to know everything. I think he’s a natural.” The two Ivy League men would become close friends, bonding over a shared appreciation for cribbage and literature.If ‘34 was a step forward, ‘35 would be Rolfe’s breakout. He hit .300 and, while he was yet to show much power, he made up for it with his acumen. He was a progenitor of the shift, keeping detailed notes on opposing hitters’ tendencies and implementing his findings on the field. The following season went even better, as the third baseman hit .319 with an MLB-best 15 triples while settling into the two-hole. He also got his first October action and made the most of it, hitting .400 in a six-game victory over the rival Giants.The Yankees settled into a familiar rhythm through the rest of the decade, winning four straight titles. And, while not able to compete with the fame of some of his teammates, Rolfe became a bone fide star, earning four straight All-Star berths and twice receiving down-ballot MVP votes. His career year came in ‘39, as he slashed .329/.404/.495 while leading the league in hits (213), doubles (46), and runs scored (139).Rolfe’s performance took a downturn after that stellar campaign. A series of health issues, including a tonsil condition, a vision issue, and intestinal colitis, sapped him of much of his strength. Rolfe hit just .250 with little pop over the next three seasons as he saw his playing time decline. He had one more shot at playoff glory in ‘42, his final season, and made the most of it, hitting .353 in an eventual loss to the Cardinals. Rolfe retired after that season to take a coaching job at Yale. In ‘46 he returned to the Yankees as a coach, and his longtime manager Joe McCarthy began grooming Rolfe to succeed him at the helm. But McCarthy found himself out of a job after the Yankees were sold to a new owner. Rolfe was forced to leave the only pro team he’d ever known, joining the Tigers first as farm director and then as manager. He took home Manager of the Year honors in 1950 as a previously moribund Detroit squad ended the season just three games back of the pennant. That success proved unsustainable, though, and Rolfe was out by ‘52. He returned to his alma mater, Dartmouth, where he served as athletic director until health issues forced him to resign in 1967. Two years later, the man who had struggled with his health throughout his playing career died at the age of 60 from kidney failure. The baseball field at Dartmouth is named in Rolfe’s honor.Red Rolfe’s statistical impact is clear and impressive. But his impact on the Yankees and the game of baseball extend far beyond that. “Red was often sought out by teammates for help with income tax filings, advice on investments, counsel on their bridge game, and even their domestic difficulties,” said the upon Rolfe’s retirement of his role as the consummate teammate. McCarthy, who managed for 24 years and won seven championships, called his protégé “one of the greatest third basemen of all time.” And he accomplished it all while dealing with health issues that would have led many others to walk away from the game. All this paints a clear picture of a player who, if you’d had the chance to watch him play day in and day out, would have been a beloved favorite, the kind of player who transcends on-field performance through strength of character. Or, in the words of the great Connie Mack, a real ballplayer.See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: Eneco Tour: Victor Vercouillie best in an all-day breakaway for first pro victory on stage 4
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Victor Vercouillie (Flanders-Baloise) won stage 4 on an emphatic day for the breakaway, taking his first pro victory on the uphill drag of Col du VAM. Cériel Desal (Soudal-QuickStep Devo) took second and Tars Poelvoorde (Lotto-Groupe Wanty) slotted into third, leaving Rick Ottema (EEW-VDK Cyclingteam) and Julian Vergouw (Metec-SolarWatt p/b Mantel) off the podium from the original group of five, the bunch two seconds behind Vercouillie at the conclusion of their all-day escapade."I went in the breakaway today because with the cobblestones and the weather, it was I think that was the best move for me and the team. That was the first plan. Then in the last lap we still [had] 1:30, that was the moment I believe in it," the 23-year-old told organisers about getting his first win."I was the last lap the whole time with my dad in my head. I lost him two months ago. That was the only thing I could think of in the final lap. So I knew I needed to go in a really late attack, and that was a perfect moment. So I think he will be proud."The GC remained consistent from Friday's shift, with Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) in control of the overall lead by 17 seconds over Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets), the final day of racing on Sunday.The three Belgians and two Dutch riders stayed away from the peloton through early rain and then blue skies for a little more than 100 kilometres, never gaining more than two minutes.On the final closing circuit with 13km to go in the 149.8km contest, the quintet held a gap of just over a minute. All five riders in the breakaway were looking to score a first career. It was Vercouillie who launched the decisive attack on the final 1,000 metres, signaling to the sky as he crossed the line with a small gap in recognition that he raced for his father who died earlier this year.Victor Vercouillie (Bel) Team Flanders- BaloiseCeriel Desal (Bel) Soudal Quick-Step Devo TeamTars Poelvoorde (Bel) Lotto- Groupe WantyRick Ottema (Ned) Eew-Vdk CyclingteamJulian Vergouw (Ned) Metec- Solarwatt P/B MantelChristophe Laporte (Fra) Visma-Lease a BikeJoeri Schaper (Ned) Soudal Quick-Step Devo TeamPepijn Reinderink (Ned) Soudal-QuickStepVictor Campenaerts (Bel) Visma-Lease a BikeFinn Fisher-Black (NZl) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheWessel Mouris (Ned) Unibet Rose RocketsCasper Matyáš Kopecký (Cze) Unibet Rose RocketsTim Merlier (Bel) Soudal-QuickStepHartthijs De Vries (Ned) Unibet Rose RocketsJakob Söderqvist (Swe) Lidl-TrekMilan Lanhove (Bel) Team Flanders- BaloiseFlorian Senechal (Fra) Alpecin-Premier TechSimon Goossens (Bel) Alpecin-Premier Tech Development TeamJonas Rutsch (Ger) Lotto-IntermarchéGerben Thijssen (Bel) Alpecin-Premier TechOtto Van Zanden (Ned) Parkhotel ValkenburgSteffen De Schuyteneer (Bel) Lotto-IntermarchéDanijel Agricola (Ned) Metec- Solarwatt P/B MantelJesse Kramer (Ned) Beat Cc P/B SaxoJochem Kerckhaert (Ned) Beat Cc P/B SaxoSebastian Grindley (GBr) Lidl-Trek Future RacingLukáš Kubiš (Svk) Unibet Rose RocketsVictor Campenaerts (Bel) Visma-Lease a BikeWessel Mouris (Ned) Unibet Rose RocketsFinn Fisher-Black (NZl) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheCasper Matyáš Kopecký (Cze) Unibet Rose RocketsPepijn Reinderink (Ned) Soudal-QuickStepMilan Lanhove (Bel) Team Flanders- BaloiseChristophe Laporte (Fra) Visma-Lease a BikeJakob Söderqvist (Swe) Lidl-TrekPierre Thierry (Fra) TotalenergiesSteffen De Schuyteneer (Bel) Lotto-IntermarchéThe road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Eneco Tour Women: Letizia Borghesi powers clear on cobbles for memorable win on stage 4
item.author: cyclingnews@cyclingnews.com (Cyclingnews)
item.content:encoded: Letizia Borghesi (AG Insurance-Soudal) claimed the second victory of her career and her first in seven years with a powerful punch on the Col du VAM on stage 4 of the Eneco Tour Women.The Italian, whose only previous career victory came with a stage of the 2019 Giro d’Italia, stomped clear of the rest of the favourites on the steep cobbled section of the climb, which is built on a rubbish dump on the otherwise flat landscape of Drenthe in the Netherlands.Pfeiffer Georgi (Picnic-PostNL) made a late burst to take second place on the stage, with race leader Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) coming up for third place to retain her orange jersey.Only around 15 riders remained in the lead group as they approached the foot of the Col du VAM for the seventh and final time on the 115km circuit-based course. Julia Kopecky led the way in on behalf of her SD Worx teammate and Nooijen’s closest challenger, Femke Markus, but Borghesi snuck in behind with a bold move through a right-hand bend.Nooijen was the first of the favourites to hit the front inside the final kilometer, but Borghesi soon made her move powering clear on the smooth cobblestones and dropping the race leader in the process. She opened a small gap by the top of the first section of the climb, and extended it with some aggressive cornering on the short downhill, which was made treacherous by the rain.Although the chasers started to close in on the final haul to the line in the last 250 metres, Borghesi had done enough to take out a memorable victory. Georgi crossed the line in second place four seconds down, just ahead of Nooijen.With one stage remaining, Nooijen retains her overall lead, extending her margin over Markus by six seconds to now stand at 38 seconds. Borghesi’s win saw her jump four places onto the overall podium at 39 seconds.Letizia Borghesi (Ita) AG Insurance-SoudalPfeiffer Zara Georgi (GBr) Picnic PostNLLieke Nooijen (Ned) Visma-Lease a item.title: Track World Championships: Yet more gold medals for Great Britain on Day 4 as Iúri Leitão takes emotional Omnium victory
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Four more rainbow jerseys were handed out on the penultimate day of the 2026 UCI Track World Championships, with yet more success for Great Britain's women.Anna Morris claimed her third gold medal of these Championships with victory alongside Erin Boothman in the Madison. Elsewhere, it was an all-British final in the Individual Pursuit, with Millie Couzens getting the better of Josie Knight. Saturday's medal events were kickestarted by Pauline Grabosch taking Germany's first gold of the week in the women's time trial, beating the Dutch reigning world champion Hetty van de Wouw to the win.The day's action ended with the men's Omnium, where Iúri Leitão (Portugal) capped a fine day's racing with a consummate performance in the fourth and final event, the points race. Read on for our round-ups of all the medal events, along with the results.The first medal event of the day came with the women's time trial, and there were few surprises among the eight competitors, with the top spots following on from the qualifying results at the start of the day.Qualifying saw Pauline Grabosch (Germany) top the timesheet ahead of reigning world champion Hetty van de Wouw (Netherlands) and 2024 world champion Iana Burlakova (Independent Neutral Athletes). The top two once again proved to be the two quickest in the final, with Grabosch's time of 1:04.572 a good seven-tenths of a second quicker than Van de Wouw, who had been provisional leader.The Dutch racer settled for silver then, while her teammate, Sofie van Rooijen, nabbed bronze. Van Rooijen had topped the standings as the fourth rider to start, and both Mathilde Gros (France) and Burlakova failed to beat that 1:05.398 run despite both starting out quicker. Burlakova finished the race in fourth place, just 0.033 seconds off Van Rooijen.Pauline Sophie Grabosch (Germany)Hetty Van de Wouw (Netherlands)Iana Burlakova (Neutral Athlete)Sofie Van Rooijen (Netherlands)Claudia Marcks (Australia)Stefany Lorena Cuadrado Florez (Colombia)Marie Louisa Drouode (France)Yuli Paola Verdugo Osuna (Mexico)Hayley Yoslov (United States)Lowri Thomas (Great Britain)Clara Schneider (Germany)Sára Kateřina Peterková (Czechia)Anna Jaborníková (Czechia)Andrea Robles Felix (Mexico)Kayla Hankins (United States)Javiera Garrido Muñoz (Chile)Iúri Leitão (Portugal) claimed the second Omnium world title of his career with a poised and powerful day of racing in Shanghai. All four Omnium events took place on Saturday and Leitão made the perfect start with victory in the scratch race by a lap over the rest of the field. Third place in both the tempo race and the elimination race ensured he entered the final points race at the top of the leaderboard, and he managed a tricky race extremely well to take the overall title. It was Tim Torn Teutenberg (Germany), winner of the tempo race, and Henry Hobbs (Great Britain), winner of the elimination race, who were the closest challengers going into the points race, with everything to play for. That much became clear half-way through the 100-lap race, when Fabio Van Den Bossche (Belgium) attacked and, after working his way through a fragmented bunch, was awarded a lap gain that gave him 20 points and put him top of the leaderboard, with points scored in the points race simply added to the riders’ totals from the previous rounds. Leitão arguably should have been more alert to it but he didn’t panic and with 35 laps remaining he made amends with a swift attack and an utterly clinical lap gain completed in just a few revolutions of the track. From there, back on top, he managed the race astutely, marking moves from Van Den Bossche, Teutenberg, and the Spaniard Sebastian Mora, who’d moved into a podium position with a lap gain of his own around the same time.Teutenberg won the penultimate sprint to move back into bronze medal position at the expense of Mora, and from there all Leitão had to do was cross the line, such was his lead with 10 points remaining for the final sprint. He finished on 143 points for the competition, with Van Den Bossche taking the silver medal on 129 points and Teutenberg clinching bronze on 115 points. Men's Omnium Scratch RaceFabio Van den Bossche (Belgium)Oscar Nilsson Julien (France)Tim Torn Teutenberg (Germany)Henry Hobbs (Great Britain)Sebastian Mora Vedri (Spain)Daniel Staniszewski (Poland)Keegan Hornblow (New Zealand)Ilya Savekin (Neutral Athlete)Clever Jose Martinez Moros (Venezuela)Ricardo Peña Salas (Mexico)Yanne Dorenbos (Netherlands)Tomas Eloy Moyano (Argentina)Alisher Zhumakan (Kazakhstan)Grant Koontz (United States)Tim Torn Teutenberg (Germany)Sebastian Mora Vedri (Spain)Henry Hobbs (Great Britain)Fabio Van den Bossche (Belgium)Keegan Hornblow (New Zealand)Daniel Staniszewski (Poland)Yanne Dorenbos (Netherlands)Oscar Nilsson Julien (France)Clever Jose Martinez Moros (Venezuela)Alisher Zhumakan (Kazakhstan)Ricardo Peña Salas (Mexico)Ilya Savekin (Neutral Athlete)Tomas Eloy Moyano (Argentina)Grant Koontz (United States)Men's Omnium Elimination RaceHenry Hobbs (Great Britain)Tim Torn Teutenberg (Germany)Fabio Van den Bossche (Belgium)Yanne Dorenbos (Netherlands)Sebastian Mora Vedri (Spain)Daniel Staniszewski (Poland)Clever Jose Martinez Moros (Venezuela)Oscar Nilsson Julien (France)Ilya Savekin (Neutral Athlete)Keegan Hornblow (New Zealand)Tomas Eloy Moyano (Argentina)Alisher Zhumakan (Kazakhstan)Ricardo Pena Salas (Mexico)Fabio Van den Bossche (Belgium)Tim Torn Teutenberg (Germany)Sebastian Mora Vedri (Spain)Henry Hobbs (Great Britain)Oscar Nilsson Julien (France)Yanne Dorenbos (Netherlands)Daniel Staniszewski (Poland)Keegan Hornblow (New Zealand)Clever Jose Martinez Moros (Venezuela)Alisher Zhumakan (Kazakhstan)Ilya Savekin (Neutral Athlete)Ricardo Pena Salas (Mexico)Tomas Eloy Moyano (Argentina)Great Britain's storming World Championships continued with victory in the women's Madison. This was hardly the most experienced pairing in the field, with Anna Morris only competing in her first Madison a year ago and teaming up with the teenager Erin Boothman. But Morris has been a revelation of these Championships, claiming her third world title of the week, and she was riding with a former junior world champion in the discipline. The key moment came with 40 of the 120 laps remaining. Until that point, New Zealand were heading up the leaderboard thanks to points gained in the sprints but despite botching a handover, Britain launched straight into a two-up attack with France, and it resulted in a lap gain and 20 points for both nations. Britain marked everything and even scored well in the sprints, taking the 10th of the 12 sprints to extend their lead over France to nine points with 20 laps to go. From there, they managed the latter phase of the race calmly – there we no more lap gains and Britain marked France on the penultimate sprint to make virtually sure of it. In the end, they finished on 40 points, beating France by seven points, with Japan taking the bronze medal with 18 points."We are actually quite fresh together. My first Madison was only in September last year so I'm not sure who's taking the lead on experience, but it's really exciting to work with Erin and hopefully there's more to come as we keep working on the partnership," said Morris.Another event, another gold medal for Great Britain's women, and this one was a dead cert as the final began. Having been the top two in qualifying, Mille Couzens and Josie Knight – who won gold together in the team pursuit earlier in the week – faced off against each other in the final, and Couzens came out on top. Couzens had qualified fastest in the morning session, just under two seconds faster than Knight, and there was an enormous gulf to the rest of the competition, with the third and fourth from qualifying – Martina Alzini (Italy) and Lisa Klein (Germany) – being nine seconds slower than Couzens' benchmark. Come the final, Couzens made the stronger start and opened a commanding lead. Knight did come back at her in the second half of the pursuit, but it wasn't enough. Couzens stopped the clock on 4:21.505, half a second up on her teammate. "I'm still a bit shocked. I had zero expectations coming in. I thought a podium would be a good result, but I didn't expect this, so I'm very happy. "It's always a bit weird racing against a teammate, but it was quite nice, you feel like you're in it together."In the bronze medal match, Klein was a runaway winner against Alzini. Millie Couzens (Great Britain)Josie Knight (Great Britain)Felicity Wilson-Haffenden (Australia)Jasmin Liechti (Switzerland)Kristen Faulkner (United States)Megan Barker (Great Britain)Luca Vierstraete (Belgium)Sophie Edwards (Australia)Anna Hicks (United States)Martyna Szczęsna (Poland)Annika Liehner (Switzerland)Katrijn De Clercq (Belgium)Tamara Szalinska (Poland)Maite Ibarra Ramirez (Chile)Ida Ayu Manik Laksmi Dewi (Indonesia)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: What drives Bortoleto as his junior rivals hit new heights in F1
The top five Yankees’ pitching performances of 2026
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: While the 2026 Yankees season has come to a frustratingly early end, it’s hard to blame much of that on the starting pitching. By several measures, the Yankees had one of the best rotations in all of baseball this year, and they have the favorite for the AL Cy Young Award in Cam Schlittler.As part of our season in review, let’s take a look back at some of the rotation’s best efforts of the year. To do that, we’re going to rank them according to the Game Score statistic. Game Score takes a variety of stats from an outing and combines them to try and determine how dominant a pitcher’s outing. Fifty is generally about average, and if a pitcher nears 100, they’re probably putting up an all-time great outing. While we didn’t get any no-hitters or perfect games this year, the Yankees’ rotation still had its fair share of excellent outings, let’s look back at the best of them.This is a post of the top five, but there was a three-way tie for fifth, so it’ll actually include two bonus games too.T5. Cam Schlittler 78 vs. Rays – July 6thOne could hope that Schlittler’s Game 2 start in the ALDS against the Rays harkened back to a regular season outing he had against Tampa Bay. Facing the Rays on July 6th, Schlittler allowed one run on four hits, while striking out eight in eight innings. None of the hits he allowed were more than a single, it’s just that one of them was to the speedy Chandler Simpson, which led to him scoring on another single.Sneaking onto the list as part of that three-way tie for fifth is, surprise, another Schlittler start. This is the only game on the list that the Yankees ended up losing, but you can hardly blame that on the Yankees’ Cy Young candidate. In his seven frames, he held Atlanta to one run on three hits while striking out 11. Thankfully the Yankees scored a run in the eighth and the loss came in extra innings, so Schlittler didn’t get dinged with a loss for that gem.You’ll never be able to guess who the pitcher who had the other game tied for fifth is…While it wasn’t as statistically dominant as his start against the Red Sox in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler’s 2026 outing was still plenty good enough to crack this list. He only went 6.1 innings this time around, but held the Red Sox to just two hits, while striking out 10. The Yankees’ lineup poured it on late on route to a win and an eventual dominant sweep of Boston. If only the rest of the postseason went that well…Someone else has finally made an appearance on the list. Injuries limited Fried to just 112.2 innings this season, but statistically he was still very good. This performance against the Red Sox was part of that. Having been given a 3-0 lead to work with after the top of the first, Fried proceeded to go eight scoreless innings, allowing just three hits and two walks, striking out nine Boston batters.Normal service has resumed as Schlittler matched Fried to tie for third place. However, this was another game where he ended up with a no decision thanks to the offense. In eight innings, Schlittler held the Angels to one run on two hits, striking out nine. The only issue was that one of those hits was a Vaughn Grissom homer that tied the game at one in the seventh inning. The Yankees eventually broke through with five runs in the top of the 10th inning to seal the win, although they deprived their ace of the victory.T1. Cam Schlittler: 84 vs. Phillies – July 24thAs it turned out, there was also a tie for first and, yes, Schlittler was involved. In July, he held a potentially very powerful Phillies’ lineup to no runs in 7.1 innings, surrendering just three hits all game. He struck out 12 batters, including Trea Turner and Bryce Harper twice each.Tying Schlittler for the top spot is a Rodón start that had people wondering what order the playoff rotation should go in. Against the Rays in late September, Rodón threw eight shutout frames, allowing just three hits in arguably his best ever start as a Yankee. He also reached a milestone in getting to the 1500 strikeout mark during the outing.The start — and his stretch run in general — was good enough that it led to people suggesting that Rodón should get the ball for one of the AL Wild Card Series games. In the end, they went with Schlittler, Fried, and Gerrit Cole had their been a Game 3. As it worked out, Rodón didn’t end up pitching at all in the playoffs. You can debate whether that should’ve been the case, but it’s hard to blame any of the starting pitchers for their ALDS losses.Those are the best starts of the year according to Game Score, but which ones were the most memorably good to you?
