item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘New York will explore other deals this weekend and Monday’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: No more fake basketball for the next eight months, folks!The Knicks wrapped up the preseason with their most solid performance, defeated the Raps in New York, and will next see the banner(s) rise to the rafters of MSG.Here’s the latest from everybody and their mothers.On the Knicks’ progress over the past year heading into their title defense:“I’m going to keep it real that there’s something in front of us. I’m not a fan of having an elephant in the room. I’ll address it: It’s about the process. It’s not about the end result. We can’t think about the end result right now. We have a ways to go. This is a new season, new team and we’re gonna have challenges in front of us.“It’s like climbing a mountain. Sometimes you go a 100 yards, but you might get knocked back five yards. Hopefully, it’s not 50 yards, but you might get back five or 10 yards, and you regroup as a team, and you figure out how to keep going forward the right way.“But making sure we embrace the process without slippage in that is going to be huge. And if I see us slipping up, it’s my job to let us know as a team that we’re off track. We need to get back on hopefully sooner than later.”On why Jalen Brunson is the NBA’s best leader, as voted by GMs:“He studies the game, and that helps a lot because you can always grow in any field you do. But he walks the talk. He works extremely hard, and he strives for perfection from himself. And when you do that, your peers see you do that, and you’re looked upon as the best player on the team, and it gives you credibility to tell somebody else when they’re not given their all or when they need to do this a little bit better or that a little bit better.”On Brunson’s toughness and willingness to hold teammates accountable:“He’s not afraid because, as a leader, sometimes you can be on an island because you have to always be conscious of ‘I got to do more, I got to do more’ in terms of work harder, focus, everybody’s going to make mistakes, but those little things. And so when you tell your teammates, they can get pissed at you, or they can be like, ‘hey, screw him because who is he to tell me what to do?’ And so you have to have some thick skin because it’s not going to always be you telling somebody to do something, then they embrace it. And I think Jalen has that thick skin and a toughness about him to be in a seat like this.”On Brunson potentially becoming an NBA head coach after his playing career:“I think Jalen has that thick skin and toughness about him to be in a seat like this. You won’t need to, though. My view? If you don’t want to… It’s up to you, Jalen.”On what he expects from the Knicks’ final roster spot:“If one of those guys makes our team, at least right now, they may not even play seven minutes — you know, seven straight minutes. And then at the end of the day, we just have to make a decision.”On the mentality required from the Knicks’ third-string center:“We just hope that there’s a passion and an energy and a focus coming from that spot because, I’m sure at times that person will start, at times they may be the first backup and at times they may be second backup. So as the minutes are fluctuating, you’re going to have to generate some internal energy at times, to go play in a low-minute game.“Sometimes he’ll maybe not play one or two, maybe three games in a row. You look for that, and then you know, you just look for somebody that’s going to play hard at the end of the day – try to do the things that you’re asking on both sides of the floor. And bring a little something different than what the two guys in front of you bring.”On Bruce Brown’s experience, toughness and versatility:“Bruce has been through a lot with a lot of different teams at a pretty high level. His toughness, his experience, his feel, all those things — he’s a winner. It seems like every place he’s gone, he’s won, but all those things can add a lot to the program, and then he’s versatile both ends of the floor. He could play a few different positions offensively; he can guard a few different positions defensively. So a guy like that, especially a veteran winner, can be helpful to any team.”On James Wiseman’s potential and development:“He’s young, he’s talented, you know, he’s raw, still. I think he’s still trying to establish a foothold in this league. But with the God-given attributes he has, in terms of athleticism and length and quickness, [they] can bode well for him on both ends of the floor. And at 25 years old, he hasn’t even reached his prime, especially knowing he hadn’t played a ton of basketball; having a vertical threat at the rim will help [the Knicks], or could help everybody else play the game a little bit easier, whether it’s driving the basketball or playing pick and roll.”On his recovery from wrist surgery:“I had nine different casts. I was able to take it off if I ran or worked out with it. So I had one for workouts, one for showering and obviously one for everyday use.”On maintaining the Knicks’ championship-winning approach entering a new season:“I think what’s most important is that last year we took everything one day at a time. We were talking about — obviously, the topic was getting back to the conference finals and trying to advance. And I think for us now, the way we approached it last year was to take it one day at a time, every single day. So not talking about certain things.“Obviously, we know what it takes, but just going into this with the same mindset for this journey. Even though it’s a new journey, it’s a different journey; the approach has to be the same, if not better.“The first couple of weeks of the season is going to show us who we are and where we are. No matter what we’re doing, whether we’re playing great, playing bad, how are you going to be able to learn? And so, I mean, we’ll find a way. We’ll hold each other accountable, just like we did last year, and then we’ll be better.”On the Knicks’ preseason progress and preparing to defend their championship:“Each game got better and better. Just happy to be back. I feel like it’s a learning experience for us. We have to turn the page on last year and figure out how to get better every single day. It’s gonna be a different journey for us. Our mindset has to be different, and we’ll be ready to go.”On the Knicks’ preseason finale and preparing for opening night:“I thought today was a good dress rehearsal. It was cool, it was very nice to get back out there and get back into our flow and be really good. Obviously we have a lot of things to work on. But it was a good way to end the preseason.”On how he feels physically and his rhythm entering the regular season:“Yeah, I feel good. I feel really, really good.”On who’s the biggest complainer to referees among Knicks:“Josh Hart. Why’d y’all laugh? Did y’all agree with that or something? Everyone behind the camera, I just want y’all to know: y’all just clowned Josh Hart. That’s crazy for y’all to say — in New York, too.”On choosing between winning another NBA championship and a World Series:“Win a World Series, for sure. I already won an NBA championship.”“Before the game starts, I always give everyone at the table, including the fans behind, a chance to really get into the game. Just giving everybody a fist bump down the line of the table, and then go on the court.”On his favorite all-time big man:“I think Hakeem. I feel like, in a way, he kind of is mythical, like Wilt Chamberlain… but I’ve been able to talk and meet Hakeem, and he’s an amazing, amazing human.”On the Knicks’ roster decisions involving Bruce Brown, James Wiseman, Pacome Dadiet and Tyler Kolek:“Brown and James Wiseman have made it through preseason cuts. The Knicks clearly like both players. But New York only has room under the second apron in team salary to keep one player. In order to keep both Brown and Wiseman, the Knicks would need to trade a player on a standard contract without taking back salary. “My read heading into the weekend: Wiseman is a lock to make the roster. There is strong support to add Brown as well. The Knicks would need to make a trade by Monday afternoon if they want to keep Brown. I think they will explore all avenues to make that happen. “It’s logical to assume that the Knicks will move third-year wing Pacome Dadiet. But I believe New York will explore other deals — including trades involving third-year guard Tyler Kolek — this weekend and Monday. “The Knicks will be asking teams to take on a player without sending back salary. To get a deal done, New York may need to attach its own second-round picks (New York will have at least 11 second-round picks in the next seven drafts).”On the Knicks’ handling of Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract negotiations:“So, it was smart to dead the conversation. Now, how you deaded the conversation is the problem. I can’t find out on Twitter if that’s what happened…So if that’s the case (Towns learning from the media that the Knicks paused negotiations), then that’s a communication thing right there. [The Knicks] dropped the ball on that one for one. You don’t let that get outside. So again, I don’t know that. The only thing I’m saying is you don’t break up the family. That’s all I’m going to say. You don’t break up the family.”On fulfilling his childhood dream of becoming a police officer:“It’s something I always wanted to do since I was a kid. I remember back when I was in grade school, elementary school. They asked you on career day, ‘What do you want to be when you grow up?’ And my initial response was a police officer.”On his family’s history in law enforcement:“It runs in the family. My uncle was a captain. His brother was a deputy. My cousin is a captain. My sister’s in the academy. So, it’s a family tradition, basically.”On the physical demands of police academy training compared with the NBA:“Yeah, it was a little bit [more] challenging actually because now I’m running a lot more than I had before. Obviously, in the NBA you run short distances, right? And the police academy, you’re running more long-distance mileage.”On his wife’s initial concerns about his decision to become a police officer:“My wife at first was a little bit concerned because obviously being a police officer, there’s some danger to it. But if you are well-trained and you understand your policies and procedures, you’re able to somewhat have officer safety, which is very important, and that’s the goal.”

item.title: Which mountains will be on the 2027 Tour de France route? Pyrenees back to the fore, one ferociously difficult stage, and other emerging details
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: The 2027 Tour de France looks set to have its major mountain showdown in the Pyrenees next year, with a summit finish on the notoriously difficult Col du Portet a frontrunner to finish off what could well be the toughest single climbing stage of the race.Described back in 2021 by Tadej Pogačar as a "never-ending story," according to La Nouvelle République des Pyrénées, this time round the Col du Portet could be preceded by two historically famous Hors Catégorie ascents, the Tourmalet and Aubisque, making for a ferociously difficult stage.2027's Tour is widely reported to see the Pyrenees taking over from the Alps in 2026 as the scenario for next July's main climbing challenges, with stages 18 and 19 likely the key dates in the country's southernmost mountain range.Other rumours about the major peaks of the 2027 race include an ascent of the Jura's highest paved mountain pass, Le Grand Colombier, as the curtain-raiser to the Tour's climbing stages at the end of the first week. However, as the date of the route publication on Thursday October 22 in Paris looms fast on the horizon, the most striking mountain rumours are the possible inclusion of the Col du Portet. Less famous than the Tourmalet or Aubisque, but also ranked Hors Categorie, the Portet's viciously irregular slopes first appeared in the 2018 Tour. That year it was the finish of one of the Tour's shortest-ever mountain stages - just 65km long - that saw Nairo Quintana take his last ever victory in the race. The Tour then returned to Col du Portet in 2021, when the top favourite both now and then, Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), won the stage ahead of Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) and simultaneously further cemented his considerable overall lead. With Pogačar very likely looking to fight for a record-equalling sixth Tour in 2027, the odds of a repeat battle next summer with the Dane on the same 16.2-kilometre ascent, with many segments at over 9%, are not small. Although the date for the possible ascent of Col du Portet is provisionally said to be stage 18, another day's racing is also expected in the Pyrenees 24 hours later. But in stark contrast to stage 18, no information has yet been leaked regarding potential climbs for stage 19. However, it would seem likely that the stage takes place at the western end of the mountain range, prior to the final weekend's return to Paris.Overall, as reported by , the specialist website in Tour de France pre-route publication news, the first week of the race looks much easier than in 2026. This July saw the Pyrenees feature, albeit briefly, as soon as stage 3, then again in a much fuller format across the Tourmalet to Gavarnie-Gèdre on stage 6.Next summer after the transfer from Cardiff following three stages in Britain and a long hike across northern France, the first summit finish could be on stage 9 at Le Grand Colombier. Another very irregular climb with stretches at 20% in places, the last ascent of the HC climb in the Jura in 2023 saw Vingegaard and Pogačar maintain their stalemate at the top of GC.There were seven stages in the Alps in 2026, and far fewer are expected in 2027, but the few opportunities there will likely be memorable ones all the same. After a rest day in the northern Alps, racing is expected to resume on stage 10 with a visit to the famous World Championships circuit in Sallanches. The circuit's principal challenge, the Côte de Domancy, is both where Hinault took one of the toughest ever Worlds in 1980, and also a preview for the World Championships of 2027, with two highlights being the elite men's road race taking place on the same course next August 28 and the equivalent women's event a week later.Major Alpine finishes are expected on stage 11 and possibly stage 12, with Le Dauphiné Libéré reporting that the first day could see a finish at the Col de Samoëns 1600. Part of the same Grand Massif range which contains the much better-known Col de Joux Plane, the Samoëns climb is a relatively benign 11 kilometres long, and its 900 metres of climbing are relatively steady. The same goes for the next day's predicted big final climb, Col des Saisies, 14.6km or 15.2km long depending on the approach road, but with a gradient never reaching more than 8%. Often used in early parts of the Alpine stages – like in 2023 when the race ended by crossing the much more difficult Col de la Loze – 2027 could be the first ever summit finish on the Saisies. However, its easier slopes once again will ensure the Pyrenees remain the crunch stages of the race.Before the Tour gets there, though, there'll be time for a very difficult stage across the Massif Central, featuring 4,500 metres of vertical climbing, according toand . It is said to finish at the airfield in Mende, which has been the scene of some memorable victories by versatile breakaway specialists like Steve Cummings and Michael Matthews in recent years. But Mende's most memorable day in the GC of the Tour remains 1995 when Laurent Jalabert and the ONCE team all but toppled Miguel Indurain en route to his record-equalling fifth overall win. 32 years later, it remains to be seen if Tadej Pogačar is by then en route to an all-time sixth success, and if anybody is in a position to stop him. item.title: Track World Championships: Great Britain adds two more gold medals on Day 3
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Great Britain continued their successful run on day three of the UCI Track World Championships, taking home more silverware, with Mark Stewart winning the men’s Points Race title and Anna Morris taking the women’s Omnium title in the Shanghai championships.In the other events, Jeffrey Hoogland took a fifth rainbow jersey in the men’s kilometre time trial, while Jonathan Milan backed up the Individual Pursuit world record he set in the semi-finals with a rainbow jersey.With three of the five days complete, Great Britain top the medal table, adding a silver and a bronze medal to their tally, Emma Finucane taking second in the Women’s Sprint and Joseph Truman taking third place behind Hoogland in the Kilo.Great Britain’s Mark Stewart won a brilliantly entertaining Points Race, beating the 2021 rainbow jersey into second place with a powerful and clever ride. Portugal’s Carlos Salgueiro was third.The race finished in dramatic style with Carl-Frederik Bévort only just failing to take a lap, which would have seen the Danish rider take the win. In the end he won the final sprint, but was just off the back of the bunch and took fourth place.Held over 160 laps of the Shanghai track, the 40km race began in restrained style, Red Walters (Grenada) and Ni Li (China) winning the opening sprints, though as the race developed Australian Liam Walsh moved into the lead, taking a lap around a third of the way into the race. However, by the time he reached the back of the bunch, the peloton was in tatters, and he was unable to consolidate, eventually losing that advantage and the 20 points that went with it.Thomas was particularly aggressive, though Stewart was stealthily picking up points behind him, and the pair traded punches all race long, while Salgueiro was closing in. The race swung Stewart’s way with 30 laps to go, the British rider winning five points, while Thomas failed to score. After a first attack from Dévort attack was brought back Salgueiro moved to within four points of Stewart with 20 laps to go and closer still 10 laps later. However, Bévort’s last gasp attempt worked in the Briton’s favour, and he took a career first rainbow jersey.Men's Points Race ResultsMark Stewart (Great Britain)Carlos Salgueiro (Portugal)Carl-Frederik Bévort (Denmark)Moritz Augenstein (Germany)Vincent Hoppezak (Netherlands)Vlas Shichkin (Neutral Athlete)Peter Moore (United States)George Jackson (New Zealand)Fernando Gabriel Nava Romo (Mexico)Dmitriy Noskov (Kazakhstan)Sergey Rostovtsev (Uzbekistan)Anna Morris took Great Britain’s second gold medal of the day, winning the Women’s Omnium, taking her first bunch race rainbow jersey after successes in the Team and Individual Pursuits.Morris rode strongly and intelligently throughout the four race event, finishing the top three of the first three events then defending brilliantly in the fourth. In the end she scored 125 points, beating Tsuyaka Uchino (Japan) and Amalie Dideriksen (Denmark), who was third.Morris moved into the overall lead in event two, the Tempo, while behind her Lotte Kopecky (Belgium) moved up the overall standings, taking second place, with French woman Victoire Berteau in third place.Morris remained attentive throughout the Elimination race, riding aggressively and often on the front, but was the last rider eliminated, with Berteau taking the sprint ahead of recently crowned Elimination World Champion Kopecky.With all the points scored in the Points Race counting towards the total, the final event was hugely important, and Morris started well, taking a maximum five points in the opening sprint with 70 of the 80 laps remaining. Behind her, though, Uchino continued to nag the Brit, riding aggressively, stealing points and closing to within five of Morris at the halfway mark. However, a five woman breakaway took all the points on the next sprint, easing the pressure, and when Uchino was caught behind a split shortly after, Morris's victory was all but secured.Women's minute, however, he was soon eclipsed but a series of faster times.Britain’s Joseph Truman staked his claim when he took 0.8 of a second out of Canadian James Hedgcock, but the pattern of the race continued when Oliviero (France), the penultimate rider to start, beat him by four hundredths of a second. But Hoogland was imperious in taking yet another title with a time of 58.713 seconds.Jeffrey Hoogland (Netherlands)Etienne Oliviero (France)Joseph Truman (Great Britain)Kirill Kurdidi (Kazakhstan)Maximilian Dörnbach (Germany)After setting a new World Record in the semi-finals, Jonathan Milan (Italy) took the rainbow jersey in the 4,000m men’s Individual Pursuit, leading from start to finish and beating Denmark’s Frederik Madsen by over five seconds.Milan was flying from the first lap, riding one second per kilometre faster than his rival and apparently chasing a second record time. However, in the final 1,000m he began to tire, and though Madsen was also slowing, the Italian finished with a time of 4:00.796, well outside the benchmark time of 3:58.85 he set earlier in the day.Continuing the battle between Italy and Denmark, Filppo Ganna won the bronze medal race, beating Rasmus Pedersen by five hundredths of a second after the Dane started the race fast. Ganna trailed for the opening two kilometres, but never ceded his advantage in the final half of the race. The Chinese rider dominated the first race, riding from the front, and though Finucane looked to be the stronger of the pair, she was unable to pass. With the pressure to take the match to a third and deciding race, Finucane tried a different approach in the second race, riding from the front, but was unable to best the irrepressible Yuan, who won the second race with ease.Japan’s Mina Sato was third, beating Britain’s second rider Sophie Capewell, in a three race thriller, winning the final race by just one thousandth of a second.Women's Sprint - For GoldEmma Finucane (Great Britain)Women's Sprint - For BronzeSophie Capewell (Great Britain)Women's Sprint Semifinal - Heat 1Women's Sprint Semifinal - Heat 2Emma Finucane (Great Britain)Sophie Capewell (Great Britain)The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Evans given a hero's homecoming after WRC title triumph
Lawson launches custom guitar ahead of the US GP
item.author: Hannah Atkinson
item.content:encoded: F1 driver by day, musician by… Thursday evening? Liam Lawson will make his debut in VCARB's Garage Sessions music and culture event ahead of the United States Grand Prix at Austin, while launching his very own custom Taylor Guitars LL30 GS Mini Special Edition. The guitar features a pink to white ombre design, and his racing number 30 in the centre.Liam has loved music since his childhood, as his Dad encouraged him and his brother to play from the age of six. Not quite the career path Liam ended up taking, though.The event kicks off on Thursday at Inn Cahoots on Austin’s East 6th Street, with the Esses Bazaar from 3pm, featuring live music, food, western wear, glam stations, tattoos and a chance to get up close and grab a photo with the team’s show car.Garage Sessions follows at 7pm, where Liam will perform live next to his former childhood bandmates, including his brother and two close friends!The wider line up features a mix of emerging talent and established songwriters like Jonathan Capeci, Scoot Teasley, Jess Farren, Alison Nichols, and Drake Milligan.Liam said: “I feel very proud to be launching my partnership with Taylor Guitars at Garage Sessions. Playing the guitar has been a big part of my life since I was young, as my Dad played in a band throughout my childhood. He encouraged my brother and I to play since we were six years old, so it feels like a full circle moment to be launching a custom LL30 GS Mini SE while performing with my brother and two friends who I grew up playing with."Music is a big part of my life, and I use it to clear my head during the season, so I'm really excited to perform at Garage Sessions where we can connect with fans outside of the track. I’m look ing forward to meeting everyone there.”With Garage Sessions bringing together racing, music, and community, Racing Bulls is giving fans another reason to get excited about Austin, and giving Lawson a chance to show off a skill that doesn’t involve a steering wheel.

item.title: Eneco Tour organisers quickly equalise prize money for men and women after Charlotte Kool's Instagram call-out
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Making a major change to the original total prize money of €17,205 for the women's race, and €63,465 for the men's race, TIG Sports & Events have now moved to close the €46,215 pay gap to zero.Kool took to her Instagram to call out the race earlier in the race, saying, "I'm curious if women get a discount at @eneco for energy? Prologue: Same start time, same distance, same energy," after Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) earned €1,490 for his victory on the opening day, while equivalent women's winner Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) won just €220. "Eneco and Eneco Tour organizer TIG Sports & Events are equalizing the prize money for men and women starting with this edition. The total prize money for women will be increased to the same amount as for the men," read a press release on the race's website."At the formation of the partnership, Eneco and the organisation agreed to operate based on innovation, sustainability, and inclusivity. The combination of a women's and men's race within a single event is an important part of this, as is the equal positioning of the men's and women's races. Both parties would therefore equalise the prize money in the coming years."The race noted how the originally planned prize money figures were determined by "the organisation following the applicable scales of the UCI for the category in which both races fall, and how "These scales have different amounts for men and women." But after Kool's comments, they decided to take action."Charlotte Kool's social media post illustrated that the discussion about prize equality in cycling was even more urgent than we already thought," read the statement. "This has prompted us to accelerate this step. Eneco and the organisation have now jointly decided to raise the prize money for women to the level of the men.""This is top class. I am super happy that it is being picked up like this and implemented immediately," said Kool. "It shows that the Eneco Tour really considers the women just as important as the men.""We organize the women’s and men’s races together and want to give both the same attention. The same performance deserves the same platform," said Race Director Roxane Knetemann. "That is why we already ensure that all teams receive a good expense allowance to start here, which is not common at all races. But that also includes prize money right from the start. It is good that we can realize this together with Eneco for this edition."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: UCI cancels Urban Cycling World Championships amid missile strikes on host Saudi Arabia
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The UCI has cancelled the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships with just over two weeks' notice due to the security situation in the host city of Riyadh in Saudi Arabia. Amid a much broader landscape of conflict in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia has come under fire from a series of attacks in recent days that have been linked to the Houthi militia movement in Yemen. In the past 10 days, the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which is where the vast majority of the athletes and staff would have been flying into, has been struck in several separate missile attacks. Both the airport and aircraft have been targeted in the strikes, which have reportedly killed 18 people and injured hundreds more. Several national federations had already taken the steps to withdraw from the Urban Cycling World Championships, which comprises BMX Freestyle and Trials and was set to run from November 3-7. Australia's federation stated on Friday that it "cannot justify exposing our athletes and staff to these risks", citing government-issued travel advice. Several hours later, the UCI and the Saudi Cycling Federation announced that the event "will not proceed" anymore. "The decision follows a joint assessment of recent developments in the region and their impact on the logistical organisation of the Championships," read a statement from the sport's governing body."The UCI regrets having to take this decision and expresses its appreciation to the Saudi Cycling Federation for their support and cooperation throughout preparations for the event. It also thanks the athletes, teams and National Federations for their understanding."The Saudi Cycling Federation reaffirms its commitment to developing cycling in the Kingdom and strengthening its partnership with the UCI. These efforts aim to support the growth of the sport, broaden participation and continue attracting major international cycling events to Saudi Arabia in the years ahead."It is not clear whether the UCI will look to rearrange the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships at some point down the line, or whether it will simply be scrapped for this year. The event was set to have a direct impact on the qualification pathway for the Olympic Games in 2028 for BMX Freestyle. The UCI stated it "will communicate shortly on the sporting consequences of this announcement".The UCI Urban Cycling World Championships were first held in 2017 and took place in Riyadh in 2025 as part of a two-year hosting deal with the Saudi Cycling Federation.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Who will win this year’s ultimate F1 dream ticket? You decide…
'Feels like a bowling ball went into my ribs' – Mass pile-up at Track World Championships sees Lorena Wiebes crash out of Omnium title defence – Video
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: A mass pile-up crash at the UCI Track World Championships forced defending rainbow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes (Netherlands) to abandon the Omnium, coming down hard in the first of four events, the Scratch Race, and taking down more than half of the bunch with her. Wiebes was riding towards the front of the pack with four laps to go when she was squeezed in between Lara Gillespie (Ireland) and Elisa Balsamo (Italy), causing her bike to slide out from under her as she lost control of the handlebars and hit the deck at high speed. Riding towards the front, 13 of the 24 competing riders ended up crashing as they funnelled down into a pile at the bottom of the banking.Twenty three riders were able to remount their bikes and finish the race after a restart, with Japan's Tsuyaka Uchino winning the Scratch Race, but Wiebes, who won the title 12 months ago in Santiago, Chile, was a DNF. The Dutch star was left with bandaging on both knees, both arms, and one of her ankles, but confirmed to her home media that she escaped without fractures. "It looks like some handlebars got tangled. From what I can see in the footage, I just held my line. I was focusing on the girls coming from behind and it felt like I was suddenly taken out," said Wiebes to in the Shanghai Velodrome."It does feel like a bowling ball went into my ribs. My knees are pretty scraped and I also have pain in my ribs and shoulder, but I think the damage after this blow is relatively minor."It's the second year running that Wiebes has crashed hard at the Track World Championships, coming down while leading last year's Madison after a botched handover with teammate Lisa van Belle.Already the Scratch Race World Champion in 2026, Wiebes was due to race in the Madison again on Saturday after the Omnium, and didn't rule out a quick return, albeit with some heavy strapping likely needed. "We have to see how things go during the day and if I can do some easy cycling on the roller trainer later," she said, having hobbled off the track gingerly with two Dutch team staff members by her side. "Maybe we'll tape up my body here and there and then we'll see."With three rounds of the Omnium complete at the time of writing, Anna Morris (Great Britain) currently leads the overall standings ahead of the final Points Race.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: 'If this is what is felt, we need to listen' – Picnic PostNL's Kemna left 'deeply upset' as he responds to allegations of culture of fear at Dutch WorldTour team
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Kemna was mentioned throughout the extensive investigation conducted by NOS Sport and In De Waaier, published on Thursday and which included interviews with 71 current or former employees at Picnic PostNL, one of them even describing the situation as "a dictatorship." But when he spoke to at the Eneco Tour, he struggled to come to terms with what had been revealed. "The only reaction I can give is that I am deeply upset. That I sympathise with all the people we have apparently traumatised—I don't know what words are being used. I am astonished by it, but it touches me too," he told ."And it also hurts me that we are portrayed this way as a team, and personally Iwan [Spekenbrink, team owner] and I too... We try to lead the team as well as possible, especially regarding safety. "I come from a culture – you know what cycling was like in the old days – that is exactly what we don't want: to have to do something you don't want to do to improve performance. We lead a team in elite sport, openly and honestly. And this is the accusation we receive... I am devastated by it."Kemna was mentioned by name in the Dutch media report by former rider Martijn Tusveld, who detailed how his standing in the team changed when – after being asked for his opinion by Kemna – he openly criticised the team's tactics at the Giro d'Italia in 2020."I became anxious. I thought: I'll keep my mouth shut and say yes and amen. And that's what I did for the rest of the years with this team," he told He said he had emailed Kemna directly last year to tell him he no longer dared to speak up and that he was not the person he once was.Tusveld also said he suffered with symptoms of depression in 2021, stating: "I also thought about harming myself."Kemna responded directly to this exchange, with a different recollection from the rider, and bewilderment after believing Tusveld had wanted to remain on the team even after the Giro incident."I have an email from Martijn Tusveld. I replied to it and invited him, and then things went quiet. Until today," he said. "I feel sorry for him, because I really have the feeling that Martijn is a nice guy; that's how I know him."But what I find a bit hard to understand is that Martijn worked with our team for several years and also clearly indicated that he wanted to stay with our team."'If this is what is felt, we need to listen to it'Tom Dumoulin's former coach, Adriaan Helmantel, also spoke in detail in the report, saying that the management looked to establish more control due to "paranoia" in the wake of their 2017 Giro d'Italia victory: "It became a dictatorship"Asked directly if he recognised himself in the stories, most of which are anonymous, and while noting how his experience isn't how it was described by the former staff members at Picnic PostNL, Kemna did recognise the need to act."Yes, I know those stories, I know the examples too. I also know which sides it touches upon. But that is not the side we are in when it comes to a culture of fear or dictatorship; I can barely bring myself to say it. I do not recognise myself in that at all," said Kemna."If this comes our way and we have no intentions, but if it is received as such, then we cannot simply look away," says the team manager. "We are deeply surprised that this can just happen. We will have to see exactly what it all is, but if that is the case, then we cannot do absolutely nothing."The team reportedly didn't respond when approached by and in person for comment, but did post a statement in response in the hours that followed. They confirmed they would commission an independent investigation into the team culture, and that it would "take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed." Kemna too is looking for clarity."I would like answers, and I actually said that I don't want to stand here to defend everything. I have already indicated that it does affect me," said the head coach."The most important thing is that I find it terrible that people have experienced this. I find that very sad, and the most important thing I must add to that is that we did not acknowledge it, we did not see it. And that we actually can hardly believe it. But it is there. Otherwise, they wouldn't say so."But on the other hand, we also see a lot of people on our team who feel really good. We have been working together for 18 years; we have a lot of different people and very different ways of reacting. If this is what is felt, we need to listen to it. I would like to enter into a dialogue."In response to the developments of the past 24 hours, the Dutch Cycling Union (KNWU) has also released a statement, agreeing with the need for the team's investigation. "The signals emerging in the reporting regarding cycling team Picnic-PostNL are very concerning. The experiences described by riders and staff members affect us and must be taken seriously. The situations described have a major impact on those involved, and they must be able to count on appropriate support," said Wouter Bos, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of the KNWU."Within Picnic-PostNL, a thorough investigation is needed into how this situation could have arisen and what steps are required to prevent a recurrence."As the KNWU, we stand for a cycling sport in which everyone should be able to participate in sports and work freely, enjoyably, and safely. We call upon everyone to report to the hotline in the event of transgressive behaviour, abuse of power, or an unsafe situation. Following this reporting and possible reports, the KNWU is investigating whether, and if so, what further steps are necessary."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: The extraordinary figures hinting at Aston Martin's pole potential
item.author: Mark Hughes
item.content:encoded: As the strains on the relationship between Aston Martin and its Formula 1 power unit partner Honda continue and speculation inevitably questions the future of the partnership, it's a good time to look at how the AMR26-Honda is actually performing beyond just the headline depressing Q1 ejections.While Sepang - where both cars made it through to Q2 for the first time - offered a ray of hope, it was dashed one week later in Singapore where Alonso felt certain the power unit's turbo must be broken, so poor was its performance. Honda later reported it could see no failure...It begs the question of just where would this car be if it had a competitive power unit? Is it a mediocre car, a rare Adrian Newey dud, with a poor engine? Or a good car with a truly terrible engine?If we look at the car's performance through the season in the accompanying graph, two things are very clear. 1) The step-change worsening of the car's competitiveness from Barcelona (round seven) to Spa (round 10) as the top teams piled on their developments while the AMR26 remained still in race one spec. 2) The step-change improvement from the car's sole update, in Hungary (round 11). But where does that updated car truly stack up in the quality of its chassis?We can break down the performances further by looking at GPS data from each track and assessing how much time the car loses in those sections of track taken at full throttle (ie mainly the straights). It's an inexact science because of the confounding number of skewing factors* but it does give an order of magnitude picture which is quite clear.The following is quite a reductive stat but a significant one. Comparing Max Verstappen's pole time at Sepang to Fernando Alonso's 12th-fastest time, the Aston Martin driver is 2.090s behind despite having surrendered 2.238s to the Red Bull on the full-throttle parts of the lap. The inference is that with power parity Alonso could've been on pole by a tenth and a half.What is even more eye-opening is that despite the huge disappointment of Singapore, where Alonso went out in Q1 convinced the turbo was broken, the car's corner performance was even more competitive than at Sepang.It's never quite that simple and we'd need to know comparable drag and downforce numbers throughout the compared speed range too, obviously not something the teams are going to release - to each other or to us. But since that Hungary upgrade, Alonso has been driving a car with a balance and poise that he has praised.But the hoped-for follow-up of a power unit improvement from Honda has not manifested. While Alonso's praise of the car on the cooling lap at Zandvoort after getting ninth-place points - "Thanks to everyone at Silverstone. Amazing. A lovely car to drive." - coincided with the introduction of the ADUO 1 Honda upgrade, the feedback from both drivers was that it had lost the driveability gains which had been made with the previous version.When we do the comparison of the Aston Martin to the pole car at each of the tracks since it got its Hungary aero upgrade, we get the following:Laptime deficit when not on full throttle: +1.310s (actual: 2.601s; on full throttle: 1.291s): 1.011s (actual: 2.487s; on full throttle: 1.476s): 0.237s (actual: 3.364s; on full throttle: 3.127s): 1.003s (actual: 3.564s; on full throttle: 2.561s): 2.203s (actual: 4.057s; on full throttle: 1.854s): -0.148s (actual: 2.090s; on full throttle: 2.238s): -0.370s (actual: 2.85s; on full throttle: 3.22s)We can derive a further set of stats from those numbers, that of an implied percentage split of the deficit between power unit-limited and chassis-limited sections of the lap for each of those tracks.: 49.6% / 50.4%: 59.3% / 40.7%: 92.9% / 7.1%: 52% / 48%: 47% / 53%: 101% / -1%: 113% / -13%These numbers suggest the car, even after its Hungary upgrade, was losing time in the corner and the full-throttle sections, but with the power unit forming the dominant part of the deficit, varying wildly according to track layout. But at Sepang and Singapore it was faster through the corners than the pole car.Although factually correct we should treat the above numbers with caution (read the small print*). But they do describe a basic outline, one in which corner performance is more than respectable, recently even very impressive.Worryingly though, as the chassis performance has steadily improved, the power unit appears to be worse with each ADUO upgrade.The ADUO 1 unit came one race after Hungary, at Zandvoort, and the deficit at full throttle increased by a couple of tenths. This may be nothing more than the respective track layouts but, as recalled, the driver feedback suggested little or no overall progress from the power unit there.Attending to those driveability issues via a turbo modification resulted in the ADUO 2 spec, which Alonso first got in Baku. This was the power unit in the car when it had such an encouraging run at Sepang, but the intricate corner-upon-corner layout of Singapore triggered it into a nightmare of terrible throttle response and wildly inconsistent deployment.If the AMR26 could magically be given power unit parity, would it really have been fighting for pole? Not until Sepang, no. Until then, the numbers suggest that since its Hungary upgrade it would have been a high Q2/lower Q3 car. But from Sepang, quite possibly yes. Even in Singapore.But again, there is a disclaimer about that. For it is quite possible that the Honda power unit's unique architecture (with the MGU-K up front, as requested by Newey, centralising the car's mass) has flattered the car's cornering performance. And that with a more powerful, conventionally configured Mercedes or Red Bull power unit, it could possibly lose that cornering advantage.But while taking on board the many cautious disclaimers, we can get an order-of-magnitude idea of the split between chassis and power unit responsible for the big laptime deficit of the Aston Martin. A much more detailed version of that picture will be at the very heart of ongoing discussions between the team and Honda and about what the future might hold for the partnership.*: Some of the deficit of the Aston Martin to pole will be track evolution between whatever session the Aston Martin goes out in compared to Q3. That track evolution will vary from event to event.If we compared the Aston Martin times to the fastest of the session in which Aston Martin was eliminated it would be equally misleading as the quick cars are typically just doing enough to comfortably get through while saving tyres and full power for Q3 while the slow cars are flat-out.The chosen downforce levels will also skew the chassis vs power unit picture (ie low wing would make the power unit look better than it is).

item.title: Eneco Tour Women: Femke Markus solos to victory as Lieke Nooijen defends lead on punchy stage 3
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) soloed to victory on stage 3 of the Eneco Tour Women, attacking multiple times to eventually move away alone 17km from the finish and hold off the chasers all the way to the line.The reduced bunch sprinted out the uphill finale for the minor placings and, more importantly, the bonus seconds on GC, with race leader Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) finishing second to defend her hold on the leader's jersey.Maud Rijnbeek (VolkerWessels) completed the stage podium in third, just ahead of Pfeiffer Georgi (Picnic PostNL). Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) survived the hilly, punchy day to make it to the finale in the main group, but had to settle for sixth on the uphill drag to the line."I’m proud of this victory," Markus said. "We started the stage with a patient approach as a team, but we quickly felt there were opportunities for attacks. So we fully committed to that. "Actually, I didn’t want to go so early at first, but I sensed a moment and thought: I’m taking my chance. But it turned into a long and tough effort, during which I kept thinking: why do I keep doing this to myself? But I do enjoy long attacks and racing like this. To also finish it off is even better."Nooijen now leads the race by 28 seconds over Markus, who started the day 43 seconds down, and will look ahead to the final two stages to try and defend her lead and take home the overall title.Stage 3 featured four laps around Sittard and Watersley, with the Schatsberg climb mid-lap and a kick up to the finish line for a fairly punchy stage. Only 88km long, it wasn't a day where an early break could be allowed to go up the road, so things stayed together for much of the first two laps, before splitting up on a climb towards the end of the second loop, putting stage 1 winner Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché) in difficulty.That split came back together again on the third lap, but the aggression didn't let up, with SD Worx-Protime in particular trying to put the pressure on Visma-Lease a Bike with multiple attacks. Nooijen herself had to get involved in the attacks to try to defend and extend her lead, but though the constant digs were wearing down the group, with fewer than 25 riders left with 20km to go, it was hard to make anything stick.Markus, who had already attacked solo earlier in the race, went away again with 17km to go, building a gap of 20 seconds. Visma-Lease a Bike and Picnic PostNL tried to chase her down, but they couldn't reel the strong Dutch rider back in and she soloed to the win. Despite not bringing her back, Visma's work did mean Markus only took five seconds on the line, so Nooijen limited her losses on GC and remains fairly solidly in the lead, after dispatching with Tas who had been at 20 seconds but lost time on stage 3.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Jonathan Milan breaks Individual Pursuit world record at UCI Track World Championships
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The Italian clocked a stunning time of 3:58.850 on Friday, and did so not in a medal ride but in qualifying. That means he still has racing to do, and that he could yet miss out on the World Championship title despite breaking the world record. He could, equally, break his own record later today when he faces Denmark's Frederik Madsen – who also qualified in under four minutes – in Friday's final. Milan broke the world record that he himself set two years ago at the 2024 Track Worlds in Ballerup, Denmark, where he clocked a 3:59.153. He has just taken three tenths of a second out of that. As with Ballerup, the track for the 2026 Worlds in Shanghai is located near enough at sea level, so there wasn't the advantage of the lower air density of a track at altitude, which comes with lower air density. Four world records fell at the European Championships earlier this year, held at a track in Konya, Turkey, at just over 1,000 metres of altitude. Milan's time marks another frontier in the progression of the men's Individual Pursuit world record, which just 10 years ago stood at 4:10.543. The four-minute mark was long seen as a ceiling, but the USA's Ashton Lambie was the first to break through it in 2021 – at altitude at the Aguascalientes velodrome in Mexico – before the Italian star Filippo Ganna nudged it down at the Track Worlds in 2022 in Paris. Great Britain's Josh Charlton took the record for a matter of hours at the 2024 Worlds before it was quickly bettered by Milan, who has now surpassed himself and become the first rider to break 3:59.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Why one F1 test day decided a 2027 driver choice
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Haas would have likely made a different choice for its 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up if it hadn't started its own Testing of Previous Cars programme last year.He became the "crystal clear" choice with his strong performance in an old-school 'F1 shootout' at Portimao, as part of that TPC run in a 2025 Haas, having fended off that competition.Asked if the logic for signing Camara went beyond him being the fastest driver in the Portimao test day, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu simply said: "He was the quickest. That was a very simple answer. Definitely, yeah. He was impressive."Camara's Portimao competition included McLaren's Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and Ryo Hirakawa, the top F1 prospect of one of Haas's key backers, Toyota - which was instrumental in Haas having a TPC programme in the first place.Together with Toyota, Haas's TPC programme had already given test opportunities to ex-F1 drivers Kamui Kobayashi, Kazuki Nakajima, Romain Grosjean and Super Formula champions Sho Tsuboi and Ritomo Miyata over the first year and a half of the project.But the biggest vindication of the TPC project so far came in August, with the Portimao shootout test being vital to Haas's 2027 driver choice."This is part of the reason why we wanted to have a capability to do a TPC [programme]," Komatsu said."Then last year was about getting off the ground, operating professionally, creating a good culture, a good team."Then this year we knew that we have to be able to evaluate drivers. We can anticipate that because of the contractual situation of our drivers [Ocon and Ollie Bearman's contracts expire at the end of 2026]."We had the capability, therefore we could assess it by ourselves. But without doing that one, I cannot be nowhere near as confident, right?"Then I don't know if I made the same decision, seriously. I don't, probably not. I don't know because Formula 2 from outside is very, very difficult to understand."All you guys were questioning when I took Ollie for a '25 seat, 'Ollie's not performing in F2 [he finished 12th in 2024]. Are you sure that's the right choice?' I had a question from many of you, but I was confident because we had access to Ollie through FP1s. I knew what he was capable of."We knew what he was capable of and what kind of personality he is etc. So without doing this TPC, if we decided to take Rafa without doing it, it certainly feels much more like a gamble."Then do I want to gamble like that? Probably not, but it's a hypothetical situation. This is why we put the environment in place so that we can take it under our control."'Equally exciting' potential to BearmanJust three days separate Bearman and Camara in age, and both will have spent five years on the junior ladder before graduating full-time to F1.Both demonstrated devastating raw pace below F1 despite some rough edges - Camara is leading the F2 championship, but there have been lost wins and podiums through incidents.So The Race asked Komatsu if he feels there are some parallels between the two: "Yeah, in terms of potential we see, I would say equally exciting. Very, very similar."But in the details, I think it's different because what impressed me most with Ollie was how he understood the overall situation, how he understood his role, how he executed in FP1 in Mexico [2023], first time in F1 car."That's a very different scenario to what Rafa had in Portimao, which was a clear, clear shootout, right? The first time he's jumping in our car. So speed, honestly, excitement about the speed, I would say similar."But in terms of how we were impressed with Rafa, it's really that judging those conditions, because you got to have a very, very good feel for the car about the grip, to be able to judge those ever-so-changing conditions."The condition was changing every minute, every lap, right? No two laps are the same. So that was impressive. But also knowing it's a shootout, how he, let's say, created his environment so that he could focus on what he needs to do and how he wasn't fixated on the outcome."He focused on what he needed to do to be himself, to get his best performance, to then understand what the mechanism for him to do that and then execute was very impressive."Other than the speed, it's like 'wow' - it's just potential how we can grow together, how we can nurture this talent, how we can flourish, is a potential. So that is the common, exciting factor."Bearman hasn't been officially confirmed as Camara's 2027 team-mate but it appears to be a matter of time."I'd like to continue with Ollie, he's an incredible talent and he showed amazing growth," Komatsu said."Then this year, he's shown that he's ready to be a team leader. Also, how he raced in Singapore [he charged from 13th to sixth in the sprint], which was very, very impressive."It's just a matter of timing [and] finalising certain details. But yes, it is our intention to continue with Ollie, but then a formal announcement will come in due course."What of the other candidates?Ocon has ruled himself out racing in another series in 2027 and is likely to take a reserve driver role elsewhere on the grid next year.Komatsu spoke highly of the three drivers Camara beat in the shootout. "The good thing of all those driver selection processes was all drivers who were involved in that did a very, very good job. Rafa, Leo Fornaroli, Ryo Hirakawa, Jack Doohan. I believe they all got the best out of themselves and every time they got in the car, they improved."So that was honestly a very, very uplifting process to be involved with."Asked specifically about Haas’s reserve driver Doohan continuing with the team into 2027, Komatsu said: "Our door's open, definitely. We've been talking with him and then his manager as well to see if we can do something together beyond this year."So that's still an open question."And given Toyota was so instrumental to Haas's TPC programme, providing both finance and engineers for it, how did it feel about Haas picking a Ferrari-backed driver over one of its own in Le Mans 24 Hours winner Hirakawa?"From the very moment we started talking with Toyota in 2024, I knew that Akio-san [Akio Toyoda, Toyota chairman] was very keen to get one of his drivers to the race seat next year, 2027," said Komatsu."So I went to see him in person, in Tokyo, before we signed anything, before he made any comment, because I didn't want any misunderstanding. I didn't want him to, let's say, invest in the team with a misunderstanding of, 'OK, if we work together, we can get one of my drivers to the race seat'."I said to him, 'Look, I understand your target, but this driver, whoever your driver is going to be, has to be the fastest one, because if I chose the driver who is not the fastest, who is not the best, they're going to be labelled as, OK, Toyota just poured the cash in to get their driver into F1'."Then whoever this driver is who got the seat, because of Toyota backing, is going to be labelled as a 'Toyota pay driver'. Then we're not going to produce the result that we should be producing, because this guy's not the fastest guy."So, for all three parties involved, it's not going to work, is it? So, I was totally transparent from the start: 'Akio-san, we're going to choose the driver who is the fastest'. And then he's completely happy with that."Initially, when we told him the plan to assess Ryo Hirakawa alongside some other drivers, he was actually very happy to say, 'Wow, Haas is doing it properly in this way'."That shows the calibre of the person, I think. He was never expecting his driver, in this case, Ryo Hirakawa, to be given a seat without merit, right? And then he was assured that we are doing it as professional and as fair way as possible that we can execute."Once I made a decision, and then I went to see him on Monday after Singapore, because we had another event, but that was a good chance for me to catch up with him."So, I told him in person with everything, all the process etc which he knew anyway. It was important for me to, again, look at his eyes in person to just tell him. He was absolutely fine. But he's that kind of person. He's great."So, I cannot be grateful enough that we have this collaboration that I actually met him."

item.title: Tour of Guangxi: Paul Magnier claims victory and the race lead as sprinters survive hilly stage 4
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: A day after losing the race lead to a mechanical incident in the sprint, Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) reclaimed the Tour of Guangxi red jersey with a fine sprint victory in Tian'e as the fast men survived the hilly day and a late crash. The Frenchman – who won every single sprint stage at this race last year for a five-victory haul – has had his supremacy challenged this year, winning on the opening day but then beaten twice in a row, but he was back to his best on Friday.He outpowered Decathlon CMA CGM's Cees Bol to the line, sprinting in place of Olav Kooij, with Max Kanter (XDS Astana) coming up in third. A big crash on one of the late corners saw a lot of riders taken out of contention, with only a reduced group coming to the line. Magnier took to the front of the sprint early and had a long effort to the line, but kept his speed and power for a good 150 metres to hold off his rivals and claim the win.With his victory, Magnier goes back into the race lead, leapfrogging stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL) who finished fourth on the day."I’m super happy, especially because today was a really hard day," Magnier said."I want to thank my teammates and the team for their confidence. I was dropped earlier in the stage, but I managed to get back to the bunch and refocus on the final sprint. My lead-out did a great job again, and I could launch my sprint and finish it off. It feels really good to be winning again and to take back the overall lead."Featuring over 2,700m of climbing, stage 4 from Bama to Tian'e was not a nailed-on sprint, with plenty of opportunities for attacks, but whilst those attacks did come and plenty of riders tried to catch the sprinters out, the sprint squads worked hard to keep things together and bring a big bunch to the line in Tian'e.A similar parcours is on the menu on Saturday, a day that is hilly early on but survivable for the sprinters, before the hilltop finish on Sunday should decide the general classification at this edition of the Tour of Guangxi.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Knicks 122, Raptors 120: Scenes from Towns toppling Toronto
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: Tonight at Madison Square Garden, the Knicks played their final preseason game—a rematch with a Toronto team that clobbered the reserves on Tuesday. This time, the fight was fairer. The visitors played their starters (Immanuel Quickley, RJ Barrett, Scottie Barnes, Kawhi Leonard, and Jakob Poeltl), but so did the Knicks (mostly: Mohamed Diawara took Josh Hart’s spot). Determined to not lay a complete goose egg this preseason, coach Mike Brown returned to his starters in the fourth quarter, and that gave them just enough juice to win, 122-120.The game started on the right foot. Resuming their championship ways, Karl-Anthony Towns took turns with Jalen Brunson on give-and-go sequences that were money in the bank. When KAT sat around the three-minute mark, he had five points, five boards, and six dimes on perfect shooting. Included in those buckets was a laser from deep. Every time he swishes the net this season will sound like a whispered, “Pay the man.”Across the aisle, Barnes converted his first four shots for an early nine points. That’s what has Toronto fans excited: four scoring options in their starting lineup to complement a top-ten defense. Neither team lived up to their defensive potential in the first frame, however. They allowed each other to shoot over 60% from all areas of the floor by the midway mark.Even Diawara (carrying two fouls) laced a corner three. Not to be outdone, Miles McBride (who had two triples through four preseason games) dropped three threes in his first four minutes. Those were positives. What wasn’t: Pacome Dadiet checking in and promptly getting stripped while over-dribbling. Soon after, he flushed a pass from Brunson, but there was nothing to change our minds about the youngster. In preseason form, the two teams traded buckets, but by the quarter’s end, the good guys were up, 35-32.Andre Drummond provided a steady hand off the bench, hoovering up rebounds (seven in seven minutes), rattling in a jump hook, tipping in a putback, and making a free throw or two. That softened the sting of seeing Mitchell Robinson doing his best Bill Russell impersonation at TD Garden. Also off the bench, Landry Shamet picked Jamal Shead’s pocket and, on a fast break, fed the trailing Jordan Clarkson. Just a few pros giving the team solid minutes.Toronto fell behind by 10, but clawed their way back by disrupting New York’s offense. Shead and Jamison Battle hit threes; the former is a defensive pest and blocked two perimeter shots (Diawara, Shamet), while Collin Murray-Boyles intercepted two Brunson passes. Towns had lost the touch, missing two threes and coughing up the rock twice. Nonetheless, New York won the quarter 28–26, and entered intermission ahead, 63-58.The hosts had shot 55% overall, 47% from deep, and had a 32-18 advantage in the paint. They’d out-bounded the Raps, 26-16, but turned the ball over 12 times, which kept them from running up the score. Top scorers through the half were Barnes (15 points) and Mikal Bridges (14 points, two blocks, 6-of-8 shooting). Bridges made all five of his two-point attempts and canned a Brunson-assisted three, but his jump-out-of-the-seat play was the block of Barrett’s three at the buzzer. I’d say Mikal is ready for opening night.With our team fumbling and bumbling after the break, the guests gained ground and overran the score, 69-66, with scores from Leonard, Quickley, Barrett, and Murray-Boyles. For the Knicks, Anunoby continued to struggle from yard, having made just 1-of-11 through the preason after his miss early in the third. Diawara committed another foul trying to grab a board, and his fourth infraction in 13 minutes earned him a quick hook.Remember when Brunson joked that his SNL episode would be like a Knicks playoff game: crappy through three quarters with a big finish at the end? The Knicks still feel like a team that can’t play a complete game. We cheered when Towns dished to a cutting Shamet for a dunk (yes, Shamet!), but no one boxed out Barrett at the other end for an easy response.Coach Mike Brown wanted this win, we gather, as he left Brunson and Towns on the floor late in the third quarter. Brunson steadied the offense, scoring seven points and dishing two dimes to fuel a 9–0 run. Dadiet made a hook to tie it at 74 (then missed a dunk), and KAT connected from deep to regain the lead. With a 19-5 run—including OG’s first basket after missing seven shots—our heroes finished the frame up, 87-79.A few times tonight, we saw Jose Alvarado and Drummond playing a nice two-man game. When Andre drove to the cup for a finger-roll, it gave the home team double-digit lead. Alvarado made his first three dingers from deep, too. We’re eager to see more of this dynamic duo. The Dinos went on a Barnes-heavy run and scored eight unanswered to tie the game around the 9:30 mark, but then Alvarado, Anunoby, and Shamet stimulated a seven-point swing to stop the insanity.The toughest move of the night was Mike Brown refusing to go winless this preseason. At 8:28, he subbed Brunson, Towns, and Diawara in to hold the lead alongside Shamet and Anunoby. OAKAAKUYOAKs Barrett and Quickley would not willingly roll over on their old home court, however, scoring their 21st and 18th points respectively. For a scrimmage, this one was competitive late.When Towns sat at 5:15, his box score read 13 points, 15 boards, and nine assists and his team clung to a six-point advantage. It would be up to the reserves to close out the dub: Tyler Kolek, Tyler Nickel, Dadiet, Diawara, and James Wiseman. Tonight we got just four minutes of Wiseman, who seems to have secured the third-string center spot with today’s annoucement that Drew Eubanks has a torn pectoral.With a minute to go, Jaden Bradley had tied the score at 117. From there, though, the Tylers combined for five points (including a trey for Kolek) that offset a late bucket by Malachi Smith. These games don’t count, but this one sure had some fun moments.Opening night is Tuesday, with a banner and the Sixers. Rest up, Knickerbockers.

item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.author: Guardian sport
item.content:encoded: Henderson back on Merseyside, Farke threatens more misery for Carrick and Forest are a threat to ArsenalA lively reception awaits the former Liverpool midfielders Jordan Henderson and Xabi Alonso at Everton and, in the case of the former, any jeers can be considered an unintentional tribute. They will speak of what the 36-year-old is able to produce now as much as what, and where, he delivered in the past. With two goals and an assist against Bournemouth last Saturday, Henderson became the oldest player to contribute directly to three goals in a Premier League game, and demonstrated his role at Chelsea is not simply to elevate standards off the pitch. His midfield partnership with Moisés Caicedo gave Alonso’s team balance and enabled the front three of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer to flourish. Their confrontation against an Everton defence that had impressed this season, only to litter the draw at Hull with costly mistakes, will provide a stern test of the hosts’ unbeaten start and may well be dictated by the veteran behind them. Everton v Chelsea, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)Brentford v Liverpool, Saturday 3pmFulham v Hull, Saturday 3pmContinue reading...
