item.title: Eneco Tour: Jakob Söderqvist doubles up with dominant stage 2 time trial victory, extends race lead
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) doubled up on victories at the Eneco Tour, adding the stage 2 individual time trial to his prologue success in the Netherlands on Thursday. In a close-fought battle over the flat 13.6km course in Tilburg, Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) had set the best time and held off a powerful charge from Ethan Hayter (Soudal-QuickStep) by less than half a second, but the Swedish rider was simply too fast and knocked him off the hot seat as the last starter. Almost crashing as getting on the power too early caused him to pedal strike around one of the final corners, Söderqvist stayed up and arrived at the line in a time of 15:04 to beat Fisher-Black by 11 seconds, also the only rider to average more than 54kph throughout his effort. With a small hop over the line, the Swede netted the eighth win of his career and sixth in a time trial as a professional, also extending his overall lead of the race to 14 seconds from Hayter and 15 from Fisher-Black. "It was a fast one, actually; I think I experienced it faster than I expected beforehand. I didn't feel too much headwind even though we were talking about it a lot before, so it was just a good day, and I cannot say much more than that," said Söderqvist."It was nice corners, kept you on your toes a bit – how I like it – and it was a bigger pleasure than normally."He'll look to defend his orange jersey in the remaining three stages, with punchy routes and some likely breathless racing standing in his way of the overall title on Sunday. Sat in eighth overall, 29 seconds down, Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike) looks the most likely rider to challenge Söderqvist for the overall."For sure I'm happy. Everything so far is as good as we could ever expect. I was strong in this race also last year, so we know it suits me really well, but I'm happy the shape is still here with me this time of year, and we hope to keep it," he said."The pressure will be on, and we know how good people like Christophe Laporte are on Vam Berg," who won his European title there in 2023, "and even tomorrow will already be a lot of pressure from the other teams who believe. We are here to fight, and this is how we need to pursue."Racing continued at the Eneco Tour with Milan De Ceuster (Picnic PostNL) leading the 87 riders off the start ramp of the stage 2 individual time trial in reverse GC order. An early benchmark was set by Steffen De Schuyteneer (Lotto Intermarché) with a time of 15:46 over the 13.6-kilometre course in Tilburg, until he was beaten by Milan Lanhove (Team Flanders-Baloise), who went eight seconds quicker. As a result of the opening day's prologue, most of the top time trial riders were placed inside the top 10 on GC, so Lanhove would have known his time was vulnerable, and it was Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) who knocked him off the hot seat by 11 seconds – but there were several riders going even faster on the course. Among those ahead of Campenaerts at the intermediate check were his Visma teammate Edoardo Affini and Kristian Egholm (Lidl-Trek Future Racing), but both lost out by more than 10 seconds after a rapid final run to the line by the Belgian.Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal Quick-Step) was the first rider to average more than 53kph over the course, knocking Campenaerts out of the top spot, with just eight riders still to come in. But it wasn't long before Fisher-Black scorched to the line four seconds quicker than the Dutchman. Hayter ran him close, missing out on the lead by less than half a second, but the prologue winner and pre-stage favourite Söderqvist was powering through the course, clocking through the intermediate check five seconds faster than the Kiwi. Söderqvist ramped up his speed and the risk, almost coming unstuck before the final kilometre, but he kept it together to convincingly beat everyone by more than 10 seconds. item.title: 'It became a dictatorship' – Extensive report on alleged culture of fear leads Picnic-PostNL to launch independent investigation
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: WorldTour team Picnic PostNL will commission an "independent, professional investigation into our team culture" after an extensive report in Dutch media revealed alleged toxic working conditions in recent years, which one former coach described as a "dictatorship". revealed the findings of their investigative report on Thursday morning, conducted over several months in 2026, into the culture that developed under sports director Rudi Kemna and team owner Iwan Spekenbrink.The two media outlets spoke with 71 current or former employees of the team, most of them being quoted anonymously, to paint a picture of an alleged "culture of fear" and an "unsafe working situation". Picnic-PostNL issued a statement on Thursday, saying "we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications", but nevertheless acknowledging that "it is important to take a critical look at ourselves" in light of the reported findings. "The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for," read the statement. "We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL."What exactly has been said about the culture in the team?The most striking claim of a toxic culture came from retired professional rider Martijn Tusveld, who raced in the team's colours for seven seasons, first as Sunweb and then as DSM between 2018 and 2024. He highlighted how his standing in the team changed when – after being asked for his opinion by Kemna – he openly criticised the team's tactics at the Giro d'Italia in 2020. Tusveld was reportedly told he was creating a "negative atmosphere" and would later tell Kemna directly, in a 2025 email, that after the Giro incident he no longer dared to speak up, feeling "powerless", and even that he was not the person he once was. "I became anxious," he told . "I thought: I'll keep my mouth shut and say yes and amen. And that's what I did for the rest of the years with this team."Tusveld also said he suffered with symptoms of depression in 2021, stating: "I also thought about harming myself."Just one account of the 71, similar experiences to Tusveld's about a shift in the team's culture were detailed by anonymous former staff members in the report.Tom Dumoulin's former coach Adriaan Helmantel was another who spoke on the record, claiming that Dumoulin's landmark victory at the Giro d'Italia in 2017 did mark a turning point for the team, but not in the way it should have. As Helmantel saw it, the management looked to exert excessive influence, wanting everything to trickle down from the top, as "they started becoming paranoid" of riders "calling the shots" if riders and coaches became too close. "It became a dictatorship," Helmantel said. In a separate report from , former rider Nicolas Roche, who also rode for Team Sky and Saxo Bank, issued a striking statement: "I think this management is not suitable for cycling," said the Irishman. "In cycling, we have to deal with a lot of variables. It is not a predictable sport. The body is not a perfect machine. We have to deal with the weather conditions and also the tactics of 24 other teams. I understand that people want a master plan to be prepared, but they cannot plan the 17th stage of the Tour de France as early as May. And that is what they did."Roche claimed that he was "pushed towards the exit" in 2021 and that he was told he had "too much influence on the young riders", stating: "My experience became a problem for the management."In their statement, Picnic-PostNL said: "If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened."Team dispute claims they didn't engage with investigationWhile Picnic-PostNL have now issued a statement and vowed to launch an internal investigation in direct response to the report from and they have disputed the two publications' claims that they refused to engage with the investigation. claim that they approached the team for comment in response to their findings on October 12, and then approached the team management in-person two days later, stating: " and gave owner Iwan Spekenbrink the opportunity at the Picnic-PostNL headquarters in Deventer to respond regarding the WorldTour team's working methods. Spekenbrink proved unwilling to do so and ultimately chose not to respond at all. Neither in writing nor on camera."Picnic PostNL have a differing view on how attempts at conversation played out once presented with the investigation, as referenced in their statement."According to , it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this."Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with . These attempts were unsuccessful."Picnic-PostNL's statement in fullWe have taken note of the publications by NOS Sport and In de Waaier about Team Picnic PostNL. The accounts shared by current and former riders and staff members affect us. At the same time, we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications.The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.The team and our three promisesSince the team was founded in 2008, three promises have formed the foundation of our approach to professional cycling.The first promise: fair, healthy and responsible sport.Our anti-doping policy is an important part of this promise. It is not only about what we communicate externally, but also about the mindset and ethical considerations that guide our decisions in practice.The second promise: safe collaboration based on shared values.We want everyone within the team, on and off the bike, to be treated with respect and to feel free to express an opinion, encourage one another, ask questions and raise concerns. Mutual commitment and integrity are central to this, helping us create an environment where people can develop, perform and enjoy working together.The third promise: continuity and job security.We have made a commitment to do everything we can to secure the future of the team and, in doing so, preserve jobs within professional cycling.While this may sound self-evident, job security in professional cycling is anything but. The sport’s economic model falls seriously short. Every year, several teams disappear, with the associated loss of jobs. This has become almost normal, even though it should never be the case in a sport of this scale.That is why we have been working to secure the future of the team since 2008. Over the years, we have provided employment for hundreds of people.According to NOS, it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with NOS to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this.Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with NOS. These attempts were unsuccessful.Independent investigation into team cultureIn a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Should you rethink the cycling kit you're buying? Why circularity could be the future of sustainable clothing
item.author: Emma Cole
item.content:encoded: According to the European Environment Agency (EEA), each European citizen throws away an average of 16kg of textiles each year. The EEA estimates almost 75% of this is incinerated or ends up in landfill, and some is shipped to Asia and Africa. The reality of this is shocking. I’ve seen it first-hand at markets in Tunisia where hundreds of tables of clothing are piled high and sold for a few pounds, and global fast fashion brands do the same thing but on a much, much bigger scale around the world. Albeit smaller than the big fast fashion manufacturers, cycling clothing is also part of this conversation, especially given the constant flow of new collection launches, designs and colourways. The UN Environment Programme says 2-8% of CO2 emissions come from the textile industry, while the Ellen MacArthur Foundation says that only 1% of clothing is circular. Circularity refers to the concept of keeping clothing in use for as long as possible, through reuse, repair, and recycling, essentially a loop, and eliminating waste. By comparison, the traditional manufacturing model is linear: clothing is sold to be worn and then disposed of, often without regard for repair and reuse. Circularity has yet to become mainstream in the clothing industry, let alone the cycling kit sector, but French brand Velor is trying to change that. We spoke to Velor and other voices in the cycling industry to learn more about the future of sustainable clothing, and how cyclists can join that movement. A world-first 'circular' cycling jersey Velor, a brand founded in France in 2021, has created the first circular cycling jersey made from textile waste, could represent a major step forward for both the sportswear and textile industries. It took five years from concept to bringing the jersey to market, because Velor had to build every step from scratch."We started from nothing, and we had to build it ourselves," says Florian Jardin, who co-founded Velor with his brother Mickael."The whole value chain is very complicated because you start with low volumes, you grow step by step, and it's not standard fabrics."The brand’s supply chain starts in France and the Netherlands with clothing collection, and heads through France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal for the final product, before closing the loop by returning to the collection stage.Velor scaled its circular jersey gradually, from lab-testing a single jersey, to recycling 300 jerseys two years ago, to now processing at the one-tonne scale.The brand also worked with Maastricht University and its suppliers to understand the impact of its jersey and to quantify the life cycle assessment data. Jardin says the result is an infinitely recyclable jersey, made from 85% textile waste and a footprint of 0.9kg CO2 equivalent. "If you look at a jersey made in China, the emissions are 3-4kg for an equivalent jersey with the same fabric, weight and construction," he adds. Another non-traditional business model is using a pre-order system, which requires customers to wait for their kit to be made, but allows brands to produce only as much as they need.Bristol-based brand Kostüme produces kits solely via pre-order. Founder Ed Bartlett says a pre-order model removes the waste which is baked into the traditional retail model. "A lot of brands are trying to solve the wrong part of the problem by focusing on recycled fabrics and repair capabilities, but the problem is we're making too much stuff," says Bartlett. "The research that I've done suggests 30% of products get sold at full price, 30% get sold at a discount, 40% don't ever get sold, and then a lot of brands have a 40% return rate, so even the stuff that they're selling gets returned, and these are big numbers. "If you can cut that by even 10% or 20%, that has a much bigger impact than anything else."Bartlett says his 55% returning customer rate and 100% year-on-year growth are proof that the pre-order model works.Kostüme also doesn’t carry the cost of unsold stock which gives Bartlett flexibility. For example, Kostüme’s bib shorts use a separately applied gripper that adds two weeks to production time and costs more but virtually eliminates fabric waste. The few items that aren't sold or are returned go to their Ready to Ship store, offering customers a chance to buy an item with a faster turn around time.Swiss brand Assos recently tested the pre-order model through a jersey collaboration with One Garment at a Time (OGAT). "The OGAT project was a way to test a new business model that brings us closer to the customer, letting us plan and produce with the goal of zero waste and zero excess stock," says Davide Colletto, quality, safety and environment manager at Assos."It is a more sustainable approach, and we are evaluating how this model could be extended to other parts of our range where it makes sense."Why aren’t more brands trying to close the loop and reduce waste?In the early days of Velor, Jardin reached out to many of the major brands in the hope of partnering with them, but he didn’t get much engagement. "I spoke to all of them, but they said they weren’t interested, didn’t have time or it wasn’t in their strategy," he says. He says cost was also a reason. Producing circular fabric costs about 11 times more than sourcing fabric from China, while manufacturing in Portugal costs five to six times more than in China, according to Jardin.Jardin built these costs into the business from the start, but for bigger brands there would be a large cost for them to pivot their business model. "The circular economy needs to deliver cheap products, and that means scaling up and getting the economies of scale", says Dr Sam Hampton, a lecturer and researcher in Environmental Governance and Behaviour Energy programme at the University of Oxford. But, as Velor shows, that doesn’t exist yet. Dr Hampton suggests a carbon tax on virgin raw materials which could be a lever to make recycled alternatives comparatively cheaper."You need to change the whole system in multiple ways, make the virgin competitors more expensive and the recycled competitive products cheaper, but that's a system-wide global challenge."The domination of the traditional model means pivoting is difficult. "The linear model still dominates the industry, but it's becoming harder to justify environmentally, commercially and in regulation," says Sam Wrest, senior ESG manager at Rapha. "Circularity is the direction we're moving in, but in cycling apparel it comes with real technical challenges."The technical challenges revolve around the difficulties of recycling mixed materials."Cycling kit relies on elastane blends, bonded seams, silicone grippers and chamois pads, which are very hard to recycle back into new fibre," explains Wrest. "Textile-to-textile recycling for these materials isn't commercially viable at scale yet."Wrest says Rapha is exploring this area nonetheless, and expects to share more soon, but its current focus remains on durability, repairs and its trade-in service to extend the lives of existing garments. Danish brand Pas Normal Studios echoes these challenges."Right now, the most effective lever within our control is keeping products in use for longer, through quality, repairs and spare parts," says Fabian Pirrwitz, Impact and responsibility analyst at Pas Normal Studios. Moving to mono-material – garments made exclusively of one fabric – is also not a straightforward solution, particularly not when it comes to technical or high-performance cycling clothing."Mono-material fabrics can make recycling easier, but the recycling and recovery infrastructure is still limited and not yet fully developed," adds Colletto of Assos. "Different garments have different technical requirements, and a single material is not always the best way to achieve the performance, comfort and durability we need."The challenges don't stop there, either. There is also the issue of synthetic fibres shedding microplastics during washing, and the long-term impact of things like PFAs, which were previously used extensively in cycling clothing and waterproofs. Whilst many brands are trying, the task of making cycling clothing sustainable and environmentally friendly is far from simple.While Velor and Kostüme openly talk about their supply chains, some brands shy away from transparency over where your clothes come from and how they are made. Several mainstream cycling brands operate with supply chains in China and Vietnam. Maap, Decathlon (Van Rysel) and Rapha manufacture some products in Asia. Decathlon brand Van Rysel has removed carbon emissions information from its website for many of its jerseys, and some of its latest products don’t have any environmental initiatives linked to them, giving the impression that the brand is scaling back on its transparency and sustainability. One Decathlon jersey still listed with emissions comes in at 4.9kg CO2 equivalent. We approached Van Rysel for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication. An upcoming EU regulation called the Digital Product Passport (DPP) scheme could change this lack of transparency in the world of cycling clothing. The DPP will require all textiles sold in the EU to include data across supply chains such as material, chemicals, origin, and recyclability. It is expected to apply by the end of 2029."I think what we need is more transparency… A name and a company for every step of the process," says Jardin.Fabric certifications such as Bluesign and OEKO-TEX are often used to imply sustainability credentials, but they're not the be-all and end-all, and certainly don't cover all factors of production."A certified fabric doesn't tell you a brand's overall carbon footprint, the full picture of how workers are treated, or what happens to products when they reach the end of their life," says Wrest. "Certifications are useful for managing specific risks in the supply chain, but they're a starting point, not proof of sustainability." A more circular and less wasteful future?With the recent record-breaking heatwaves and ongoing climate crisis, it would be logical for consumer habits to change – not just as shoppers all wake up to the impact that unsustainable consumption and business practices can have on the world around, but in response to climate change itself.Dr Hampton predicts a drive for new lighter summer kit which performs in the heat, rather than less buying overall, for example.For traditional business models, upcoming regulation will force them to pivot to more transparent practices, but the costs of going circular and lack of recycling infrastructure remain significant hurdles for many brands.However, Velor’s innovation with an infinitely recyclable jersey shows us what is possible and showcases how a circular clothing economy could work. Similarly, Kostüme’s business success highlights a consumer desire for a different way of thinking, but both Kostüme and Velor are small parts of a much wider and impactful cycling clothing ecosystem. "We’re a drop in the ocean ultimately, but hopefully we can scale this to a point where it’s inarguable, and people can’t shy away from it," says Bartlett. But with major player Assos testing the waters with pre-order, and Rapha focusing on garment longevity, perhaps the future of cycling clothing is a little bit rounder after all.

item.title: The 2027 F1 grid: Every confirmed driver
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: The 2027 grid so far hasn't brought the seismic changes some expected. Below you'll find the confirmed seats for F1 2027 so far. Lando NorrisOscar PiastriLando Norris signed a new deal keeping him at McLaren until "at least 2030" with options to extend beyond then, while Oscar Piastri has a contract in place that should keep him at the team unti the end of 2028. George Russell*Kimi Antonelli*George Russell and Kimi Antonelli were only confirmed for 2026 in October 2025, and nothing beyond 2026 was communicated within that announcement, although The Race understands both drivers have multi-year deals with various options that can be triggered for extensions.So while not officially confirmed for 2027, there's no reason to believe the line-up will change. Max VerstappenIsack HadjarBack in 2022, Max Verstappen signed a dealto keep him at Red Bull until 2028 and ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix he extended that deal to 2030.Verstappen's new 2026 team-mate Isack Hadjar received a new deal announced just before his return after a wrist injury, in Baku.Charles LeclercLewis Hamilton Charles Leclerc signed a bumper long-term deal in January 2024 for "several more seasons" and signed an extension to that earlier this year, which will keep him at Ferrari well beyond 2027.Lewis Hamilton will remain for a third year. Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon committed to racing for Williams in 2027 on the eve of the Dutch GP.Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad are Racing Bulls' driver pairing for 2026, but neither knows if they'll be continuing into 2027 yet. Lance StrollFernando AlonsoAfter much speculation, Fernando Alonso decided to stick around racing in F1 in 2027, alongside Lance Stroll. Ollie Bearman*Rafael CamaraNico HulkenbergGabriel BortoletoBoth Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto signed for Audi on "multi-year" deals back in 2024. At the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in September 2026, Mattia Binotto said both drivers were contracted at the team for 2027 and that Audi didn't even feel the need to announce the fact. Secure! Pierre GaslyFranco ColapintoMidway through 2025, Pierre Gasly's Alpine deal was extended through to the end of 2028.Franco Colapinto's form was rewarded with a new deal for 2027, just prior to the Italian GP in September 2026.Sergio PerezValtteri BottasCadillac's first F1 driver line-up of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas both signed up for the team on "multi-year" deals from 2026.: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri: Kimi Antonelli and George Russell*: Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen: Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc: Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz: TBC: Lance Stroll and Fernando Alonso: Ollie Bearman* and Rafael Camara: Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg: Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly: Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez*yet to be officially confirmed

item.title: Eneco Tour Women: Lieke Nooijen flies to second time trial win on stage 2 and retakes overall lead
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Lieke Nooijen blasted to a second time trial stage win of the Eneco Tour Women on Thursday, overcoming some fierce competition in the stage 2 test in the Dutch town of Tilburg.The Visma-Lease a Bike rider was the only competitor to stop the clock under 16 minutes over the 13.1km course, with Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime) second, more than 20 seconds down, while stage 1 winner Sandrine Tas (Lotto-Intermarché) was third, a further second back.Nooijen won the opening day’s prologue TT on Tuesday and now leads the GC standings, 20 seconds ahead of Tas, with Vinke third, with three stages left to race.Nooijen has established herself as one of the best time trialists in the peloton this year and in this company was the clear favourite to win on Thursday. However, she will need to defend her lead on the ensuing stages, all of which have short punchy climbs, though the advantage she has built may well prove enough for her to take the overall come Sunday.Nooijen had Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) not far in front as her carrot to chase, admitting that "Yes, of course, it always gives more motivation to beat her, and she was in front of me and came closer, but I didn’t catch her."It was hard, but I’m super happy to take my second victory on the TT bike here, and I had a lot of confidence since the time of the prologue," said Nooijen, with her eye on carrying the orange jersey all the way to the end."[There are] still three days to go. Also hard stages, so I think we can make a nice plan with our strong team, and also tomorrow it will be hard in Limburg, and then on Saturday on the Vam Berg, but you need to be sharp the whole race."For its third day of racing, the Eneco Tour Women took on a 13.1km ITT effort with only 27m of elevation gain, almost completely flat, with a decent wind of around 15kph that was rarely at the riders’ back, though only with the first three kilometres into a full headwind.First off the ramp was Austrian TT champion Christina Schweinberger, the Fenix-Premier Tech rider setting a time of 7:54 at the intermediate coming point and a finish time of 17:41. Second rider off was British new pro Robyn Clay (Picnic-PostNL), who stopped the clock just seven seconds slower than the Austrian, the two riders staying in first and second place respectively for some time.Eventually Tess Moerman (AG Insurance-Soudal) overtook Clay before Slovakian champion Viktória Chladoňová (Visma-Lease a Bike) managed to usurp Schweinberger, having started as the 55th of the day’s 88 starters.However, Chaladoňová was just the first of a number of faster times, with Silke Smulders (Liv-AlUla-Jayco), Femke De Vries (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Vinke all spending a while in item.title: Conflicting reports surrounding the inclusion of the Montmartre climb on the final stage of the 2027 Tour de France route
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Editor's note: This article has been updated to reflect subsequent reports published in the French press.Question marks have emerged concerning the future of the punchy Montmartre circuit that has shaken up the final stage of the Tour de France in the past two years, with conflicting reports in the French press surrounding its inclusion on the 2027 Tour de France route. The route for the 2027 Tour de France will be unveiled in Paris next Thursday, and the newspaper reported this Thursday morning that the Montmartre climb is set to be excluded, meaning a return to a traditional flat-track sprint finish on the Champs Elysées. However, this was later contradicted by separate reports from and , with both outlets reporting that the Classics-flavoured finale will be back for a third year of high drama and entertainment. In the past two years, the Côte de la Butte Montmartre has shaken up the traditional format of the Tour's finale, measuring 1.1 km at an average gradient of 5.9%, mostly on cobblestones, and followed by a tricky little descent.The organisers had already tweaked the format, extending the distance from the top of the climb to the finish line from six kilometres to just over 10km, which resulted in the closer contest between the attackers and the sprinters. This appeared to strike a better balance between tradition and the modern desire for action and entertainment. However, both editions were somewhat awkward, given that general classification timings have been neutralised on both occasions, with the GC 'frozen' and therefore finalised upon entry to the final circuit. The final stage of the Tour has for many years been processional, with riders drinking champagne and posing for photographs in the early kilometres before racing in central Paris, but any situation where proper GC racing could see positions – or even the yellow jersey – change hands, would throw that celebratory atmosphere up in the air.The last bunch sprint on the Champs Elysées came in 2023, with the 2024 edition moved from Paris entirely due to the Olympics taking place in the French capital that summer, and the Tour ending with a time trial in Nice. It remains to be seen what the organisers do with stage 21 in the long-run, but more will become clear when we see what is officially confirmed for the final day of the 2027 Tour next Thursday. item.title: How Red Bull has improved its F1 engine without ADUO
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Lewis Hamilton is calling it the most powerful engine in Formula 1. Toto Wolff says it's clearly not lagging behind. The FIA has officially labelled it the benchmark.After Max Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, the paddock consensus is clear that Red Bull’s recent gains have come as much from the power unit as from its chassis.Yes, the team's Baku upgrade delivered the downforce step and a more consistent aero platform that has put Verstappen in a super happy place with the balance.But in F1 2026, cars and drivers are nowhere if the power unit is not up to the job – and on this front Red Bull Power Trains (RBPT) is no longer playing clear second fiddle to championship leaders Mercedes.Telemetry traces and those ghost lap replays have highlighted that Red Bull’s poles have been won as much on the straights as the corners – with a top speed profile that was not there earlier in the year.As Hamilton said after being unable to challenge Verstappen in the Singapore sprint: “To overtake the most powerful engine on the grid is not so easy.”What is fascinating about this shift in the battle between power unit manufacturers – where once Mercedes was a step above everyone – is that it has happened without any hardware steps.While Ferrari has used both of the upgrades it is allowed under the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) rules, neither Mercedes nor Red Bull has brought any new homologations.Mercedes is holding fire until at least the United States Grand Prix, while Red Bull can't have anything new because it's been ruled as the benchmark engine (twice) by the FIA’s analysis.But just because there have been no specification updates doesn't mean Red Bull hasn't unlocked more performance.The story of its season, and how it's at a point where rivals are admiring what it's doing, is because it's more consistently using the full potential of its power unit.Like a car's peaky aero package that delivers a lot of downforce in a very narrow window, Red Bull's power unit shone - but not at every track and every lap.But there was no evidence of that characteristic being there regularly over the first half of the season. Mercedes looked to be in a class of its own.Looking at how things have changed, RBPT’s technical director Ben Hodgkinson told us the key steps forward are coming from calibration work – which has involved fuel supplier Exxon Mobil and Red Bull's own engineers at Milton Keynes.This is effectively detailed work to marry up power output, fuel consumption, energy harvesting, and deployment strategies.“We've sort of found that the most powerful engine that we can create has made a combustion system that is quite challenging to make sure you always get the maximum performance out of it,” Hodgkinson told The Race,“That's put an awful lot of pressure onto the calibration team to try and make sure that it's always working at that right level.”The picture at the start of the season of how things looked between Mercedes and Red Bull was also exacerbated by decisions taken at Milton Keynes to hold fire in committing to its design.It elected to keep developing longer than originally planned. This meant it was still pushing forward with its design when, ideally, it should have been doing the preparation work on durability and calibration.“At our original point in the pre-season, when we were planning to freeze the spec, we weren't really happy with the performance levels,” said Hodgkinson.“So we made the decision to just keep going, which was giving us less and less time to do durability runs and do all the calibration work that we needed to do.“We actually started the season with quite immature calibrations. But they have got better and better throughout every single race.”Hodgkinson says the improvements have never stopped and there was a “nice step of learning” between the Baku weekend and Sepang – where that maiden RBPT win was delivered.“This was able to make sure that the engine was performing closer to its best at all times,” he said.“We sort of have an engine that sometimes underperforms to what we know it can do. There has always been this prize that if you can get it performing at the top of its range for every single lap, we're going to be in a really good place.”But it's not just understanding the power unit in isolation that Red Bull has made progress this year. The F1 2026 rules have meant power units and chassis are having to work in closer unison than ever before, and this is an area where things have moved a lot at Milton Keynes.Hodgkinson adds, “There's been a much, much deeper collaboration between the chassis and the PU side.“It is about how you balance energy and deploy it, where you can harvest it and working with the drivers. I can really see how that team is just getting stronger and stronger. When we win, it really is a one-team victory - evidence of us all coming together.”Verstappen’s back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore, plus the pace it showed in Baku, have shown that the Red Bull package is not lacking anywhere.As Wolff said: “You can’t see that it’s lagging. They have done it very well. The ICE seems to be very competitive. Obviously, you can see that with ADUO, but also in terms of energy recovery and energy deployment there. It’s pretty good.”Hodgkinson thinks the RBPT is not at its peak yet – with the ever-improving calibration pointing to further gains this year. “There's still improvement to be had just from the calibration side, so I think that you'll see a bit of that this season,” he said.And then of course it must not be forgotten that a new fuel flow regime and a change of turbo boost pressure will somewhat reset the power units in 2027.“What should have been a year of refining things is kind of a year of going again on the combustion system,” said Hodgkison, who sees opportunity for gains even if RBPT remains without any extra ADUO allowances.“We've learned an awful lot about how to get the best out of this combustion system, and so the changes that we're making for next season are from that learning.”Hodgkinson is not the sort of person who is happy to rest on his laurels.“I think there's a lot that could still be got through the calibration,” he said. “I can see our engine; there's still a margin to its theoretical best that we see on dynos.“And actually, it's not all down to calibration to solve that. You can make some hardware changes that make it a bit easier too, or a bit less of a diva, to try and use some terminology that's often used in F1.“Our combustion system could be described as a bit of a diva, and we need to make it slightly easier to extract the best out of it.“So that's some of the changes that we're making for next year, and hopefully we can get a nice step on in performance.”It is little wonder Mercedes is predicting a tougher title battle than it's had this year.Wolff said after Singapore: "One thing is for sure: next year it's full-on the fight between the teams and Red Bull is part of that."

item.title: Tour of Guangxi: Milan Fretin pips Biesterbos to stage 3 victory after well-placed Paul Magnier unclips during sprint
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Milan Fretin (Cofidis) sped to victory on stage 3 of the Tour of Guangxi, claiming the longest stage of the race in a messy sprint ahead of stage 2 winner Frits Biesterbos (Picnic PostNL).With the finish line on a wide road into Bama, the sprint was spread all across the road with little room for organisation, and most sprinters in the wind early and making a desperate dash for the line.Powering up the right-hand side of the road, Fretin just held Biesterbos off to claim the win, with Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) grabbing third. Fabio Jakobsen (Visma-Lease a Bike) had his best sprint of the week so far to take fourth.Stage 1 winner Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) had the best lead-out, dropped off just 150m from the line, but as he opened up his sprint he pulled his right foot out of his pedal and lost all speed. He was swamped by the pack and left banging his handlebars in frustration as he crossed the line in 21st.Magnier's misfortune and Biesterbos' second place means that the Dutchman now takes over the lead of the race, donning the red jersey on Thursday, though a hilly day on stage 4 means he probably won't hold onto it for long.Though it finished in a sprint, stage 3 from Jingxi to Bama was an undulating and long 212km day, with four climbs in the final 60km as the difficulty began to ramp up in China.A three-man breakaway of Jasha Sütterlin (Jayco AlUla), Tobias Bayer (Alpecin-Premier Tech) and Wang Ruidong (China) went away early in the stage, with Wang's efforts in the climbs earning him the KoM jersey.Despite the profile of the final part of the stage looking ripe for attacks, it wasn't quite as aggressive as it could have been, with the leaders not caught until 20km to go with Wang valiantly pushing on solo to be the final escapee.From there, Soudal-QuickStep and Decathlon CMA CGM kept the pace high and controlled enough to discourage any attacks and keep things together for their desired bunch sprint – though ultimately both teams got little for their efforts, with Magnier's incident costing him, and Olav Kooij not able to contest the sprint. The Tour of Guangxi kicks up a notch tomorrow, with four categorised climbs and many more uncategorised ascents on a day that takes in over 2,700m of climbing before a downhill finish into item.title: Martínez has drawn back the curtain on Manchester United’s ruinous ownership | Jonathan Liew
item.author: Jonathan Liew
item.content:encoded: Defender may not be blameless in team’s struggles but his criticism goes to the heart of what has gone wrong at the clubFor those with no interest in engaging with what Martínez actually had to say, this alone will be sufficient grounds to ignore him. Already you can sense the squeamishness of former players for whom the violation of an omertà is the real cardinal sin here, a phantom limb that still tingles years after they last stepped into a dressing room. “Disrespectful,” reckoned Wayne Rooney. “I don’t feel like he’s got the right,” agreed Ashley Young. “These things don’t end well, man,” Rio Ferdinand observed on his podcast.Continue reading...

item.title: Preseason Game Preview: Knicks vs. Raptors, October 15, 2026
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: The Knicks host the Raptors (2-1) Thursday at Madison Square Garden in the final preseason game for both. Revenge? Do preseason scrimmages matter enough to call this a revenge game? Winning would be nice, though. The world champs have dropped all four of their preseason games, with the worst game of the bunch coming on Tuesday in Toronto. On the second night of a back-to-back, coach Mike Brown rested his starters and the reserves suffered a 50-point beating. Kawhi Leonard (in his first game since rejoining the Raps) scored 21 points in 17 minutes. Scottie Barnes added 19 points, six rebounds and four assists. Collin Murray-Boyles dropped 19 and nine. RJ Barrett had 17. James Wiseman led New York with 18 points and 10 rebounds while the rest of the team struggled to stay in their shorts. The takeaway? When Toronto plays its actual rotation and New York does not, the gap is wide.Toronto is built with two-way versatility and physicality up front. With Leonard and Barnes on the wing, and Barrett and Immanuel Quickley in the backcourt, they have enough talent to be a problem. Jakob Poeltl anchors the paint and remains a serviceable center.New York has spent the preseason evaluating depth pieces and managing minutes for the starters. Tonight will be the last dress rehearsal before they uncork their season on Tuesday. We assume that means the starters will play a little longer, as they get back into full game shape, and Mike Brown will use this time to get last looks at the guys hovering on the edge of the roster. Prediction? Another L to run the table, of course!UPDATE (10:35 a.m.): Drew Eubanks has sustained a torn pectoral muscle and will be out indefinitely. That’s a tough break for the center, who was Wiseman’s primary competition for the third-string spot.Who: New York Knicks (0-4) at Toronto Raptors (2-1)Date: Tuesday, October 15, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, NYCFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky
